title: 'Broadview 6' judge moves on from White House interference claims after feds' denial
summary: <p>The federal judge presiding over the conspiracy case against the remaining members of the “Broadview Six” largely closed the book Tuesday<b> </b>on a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >bid for White House communications</a> in the case, after prosecutors denied<b> </b>that any such correspondence exists.</p><p>The feds say “there are no communications of any nature from, to, or with anyone” outside the U.S. attorney’s office, aside from local FBI investigators, and they’ve made clear that “includes anyone in the White House and all components and offices of Main Justice.”</p><p>That’s despite the fact that at least one defendant in the case, former congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, had the attention of White House Deputy Press Secretary Abigail Jackson and far-right influencer Laura Loomer.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" >Remaining Broadview 6 defendants want records showing Trump administration’s influence on conspiracy case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Defense attorneys wanted U.S. District Judge April Perry to order prosecutors<b> </b>to explain how they reached their conclusion, but she declined to do so Tuesday<b> </b>in the latest hearing in the case. She said the feds know how to do their job and that “their law licenses … are on the line.”</p><p>The judge ultimately denied as moot the defense bid for such communications, meaning the issue had already been resolved by the feds’ claims. She also denied other defense requests related to selective prosecution claims, noting that “being a politician is not a protected class.”</p><p>Being a member of a certain political party could qualify, but she told defense attorneys “you haven’t shown me any evidence that that was considered here.”</p><p>The defense recently disclosed a note<b> </b>sent by the federal agent at the center of the case, in which he identified the political positions held by some of the defendants. But, Perry noted, it did not mention their parties.</p><p>Besides, the agent also described one defendant as being an “Oak Park/Oakbrook Board of Trustees Member.”</p><p>“There’s a big difference between an Oak Park politician and an Oak Brook politician,” Perry remarked, prompting smiles among the defendants.</p><p>Point being, it was hard to make inferences from the note.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/30/broadview-six-ice-trump-doj-justice-chicago-midway-blitz" >Selective prosecution claims in ‘Broadview Six’ case the result of ‘fevered paranoia,’ feds say</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Charged in the case are four people involved in local Democratic politics. They are Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt and Andre Martin, a member of Abughazaleh’s campaign staff. The feds <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >also dropped charges</a><b> </b>against two others originally charged in the case.</p><p>The group is accused of a conspiracy<b> </b>to impede a federal agent. The case revolves around events on the morning of Sept. 26, outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview during protests against the Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign.</p><p>The defendants are accused of being part of a group that surrounded the agent’s vehicle<b> </b>and pushed, scratched and otherwise damaged it.</p><p>The case is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/28/broadview-six-conspiracy-case-involving-abughazaleh-could-go-to-trial-in-spring" target="_blank" >on track for trial</a> May 26, though a motion to dismiss the conspiracy charge on First Amendment grounds is still pending. Each defendant also faces a separate misdemeanor charge.</p><p>Defense attorneys said it’s another example of President Donald Trump’s administration using the Justice Department to target his “perceived political enemies.”<b> </b>Prosecutors said any claim of selective or vindictive prosecution is “the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/30/broadview-six-ice-trump-doj-justice-chicago-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >product of fevered paranoia</a> and delusional speculation.”</p><p>The note Perry referenced Tuesday was sent by the agent to three senior ICE officials the day the original six defendants were indicted, defense attorneys have said.</p><p>“Among the 6 defendants,” he wrote, “there is a US congressional candidate, a 45th ward Committee Person, and a Oak Park/Oakbrook Board of Trustees Member.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> title: After rocky first year, Chicago’s top federal prosecutor says he isn’t taking orders from Washington
summary: <p>When Chicago’s top federal prosecutor is asked if his office takes marching orders from Washington, he doesn’t mince words.</p><p>“You should write this down,” U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros recently told a Chicago Sun-Times reporter.</p><p>“[There is] not a single case, ok, involving politics in our decision making. Full stop. Period. Zero,” Boutros said. “And anyone who says otherwise is misstating reality. And anyone who says otherwise is an armchair expert who doesn’t know what they’re talking about. Period.”</p><p>He said he isn’t done with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >Operation Midway Blitz</a>. Nor <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials" target="_blank" >public corruption</a> — he said people should “stay tuned.”<b> </b>And having reached the end of a volatile first year in office, in which President Donald Trump has been accused of weaponizing the Justice Department, Boutros said he has cases to bring “based on facts, law and the equities.”</p><p>But his first year also featured an “unprecedented exodus” of prosecutors from the office he leads, critics note. Most section chiefs left. And convictions have yet to emerge from the flurry of charges the office filed during Midway Blitz, the aggressive deportation campaign that hit the Chicago area last year.</p><p>It charged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a>, the woman shot by a Border Patrol agent and labeled a “domestic terrorist” before<b> </b>the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/operation-midway-blitz-marimar-martinez-anthony-ruiz-us-supreme-court-feds-drop-case-against-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-in-brighton-park" target="_blank" >charges were dropped</a>. And<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/11/juan-espinoza-martinez-cleared-of-bovino-murder-plot-still-in-detention-after-judge-denies-bail" target="_blank" >Juan<b> </b>Espinoza<b> </b>Martinez</a>, the man <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/22/federal-jury-rejects-bovino-murder-plot-after-called-upon-stand-up-overreaching-government" target="_blank" >acquitted of putting a hit</a> on then-<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/12/gregory-bovino-border-patrol-deportation-elcentro-california-blowing-rock-boone-north-carolina-migrants-immigration" target="_blank" >U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino</a>.</p><p>In his most extensive commentary to date about Midway Blitz, Boutros acknowledged all did not go according to plan. </div> </div><p>Boutros has praise for Amarjeet Bhachu, the ex-prosecutor seen as the driving force behind a massive corruption investigation that began in 2014. It led to the convictions of former powerhouse <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/12/21/24006969/ed-burke-verdict-chicago-corruption-bribery-danny-solis" target="_blank" >Ald. Edward M. Burke</a> in 2023 and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news/mike-madigan-guilty-verdict" target="_blank" >ex-Illinois House Speaker Michael J. Madigan</a> in February 2025.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2025/03/04/lead-madigan-prosecutor-leaving-u-s-attorney-office" target="_blank" >Bhachu left the U.S. attorney’s office</a> the month after Madigan’s conviction, before Boutros took office.</p><p>Boutros is otherwise critical of the office he inherited, though. He points to “historic lows”<b> </b>in “virtually every single metric that was tracked by the Department of Justice.” Statistics kept by the federal courts show cases were brought against 428 people here in 2024, down from 848 in 2020.</p><p>That number rose to 598 in 2025, most noticeably with a 115% increase in fraud cases. Boutros has also touted a large increase in cases brought with help from the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2023/9/27/23891321/chicago-crime-guns-atf" target="_blank" >Crime Gun Intelligence Center</a> run by the ATF.</p><p>Safer said such numbers “are largely misleading and irrelevant.” The FBI investigation that snared Burke and Madigan took several years and involved massive resources. The impact and significance of such a case is not reflected in the data.</p><p>“We need to be prosecuting organizations — as only the U.S. attorney’s office can do — who present a danger to the people of the Northern District of Illinois,” Safer said.</p><p>Boutros insists “you can do both.”<b> </b>He said an emphasis on “big cases”<b> </b>doesn’t explain the numbers he saw when he took over.</p><p>There are now 88 assistant U.S. attorneys on the criminal side of Boutros’ office in Chicago, and 25 on the civil side. There are 123 total, including in Rockford. But Boutros said his office is “on a major hiring spree,”<b> </b>with hopes of picking up “close to 50 new people” by the end of the year.</p><p>He said he’s had no trouble finding experienced applicants, contradicting the claim that Justice Department jobs have lost their luster.</p><h3><b>Boutros focused on violent crime and corruption</b></h3><p>There’s plenty of work for Chicago’s federal prosecutors to do beyond Midway Blitz. Boutros said his office is focused on fraud, human trafficking, child exploitation, violence, cartels, drugs, guns and gangs.</p><p>It leveled a terrorism charge in November against Lawrence Reed,<b> </b>the man accused of approaching a 26-year-old woman on a CTA Blue Line train, dousing her with gasoline and setting her on fire.</p><p>And last week,<b> </b>it filed a weapons charge against Jose Medina, the Venezuelan immigrant separately accused of the March 19 murder of Gorman, the 18-year-old Loyola University Chicago freshman. Boutros said he was taking “no chances”<b> </b>that Medina might walk free.</p><p>There are other initiatives, too. Boutros announced last year that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/06/04/cta-trains-violence-downtown-project-safe-neighborhoods" target="_blank" >Project Safe Neighborhoods would expand</a> to include “the entire rail system operated by the Chicago Transit Authority.” The program brings together federal, state and local law enforcement to identify pressing violent crime problems. It helped lead to the charges against Reed.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-230000" </div><p>The ATF's Amon called Boutros a “relentless leader” who “cares deeply about his role in reducing violent crime”<b> </b>around Chicago.</p><p>Boutros created a health care fraud section and touts nearly<b> </b>$2 billion charged<b> </b>in such cases since taking office. His office has also been chosen as a “lead prosecutorial partner”<b> </b>on a Justice Department Trade Fraud Task Force, targeting people who evade federal customs laws.</p><p>He’s merged his office’s national security section with violent crimes — he says he can “surge resources into that unit as needed.” And he’s merged securities fraud with financial fraud.</p><p>Finally, there’s public corruption. Chicago’s U.S. attorney’s office has long been known for taking down some of the powerful politicians in this state, including governors, judges and lawmakers.</p><p>Turns out, Boutros said, “corruption has not stopped in Chicago.”</p><p>“Public corruption is a very special part of this office,” he said.</p><p>“And our work is not done.”</p>
author: Jon Seidel

title: Illinois Accountability Commission requests testimony from Trump officials responsible for Midway Blitz
summary: <p>The Illinois Accountability Commission wants current and former officials responsible for Operation Midway Blitz to testify at two hearings as part of an ongoing probe of tactics used by federal agents.</p><p>The letters, sent Friday by the Commission’s Chair Judge Rubén Castillo, were to: Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff for policy; Tom Homan, White House “Border Czar;" Kristi Noem, former Secretary of Homeland Security; Gregory Bovino, former “Commander at Large” of Customs and Border Patrol and others, according to Gov. JB Pritzker's office. </p><p>“I established the Illinois Accountability Commission to preserve the truth and document how (President) Donald Trump and his accomplices violated the rights of Illinoisans and terrorized our communities during Operation Midway Blitz. These officials should answer directly to the people of Illinois for the chaos and violence they unleashed,” Pritzker said. “Regardless of whether these officials are still in their roles or not, the people of Illinois demand accountability from them all.”</p><p>Last October, Pritzker signed an executive order that established the commission to hold federal immigration agents accountable for their actions being in the Chicago area during Trump's administration's ongoing deportation campaign.</p><p>"The people of Illinois deserve to know how this operation was planned, authorized, and carried out — and to identify who was responsible for the decisions that led to its implementation in our state,” Castillo said. “The Commission’s work seeks to determine who authorized these actions, what safeguards were in place to protect Illinois residents, and what accountability mechanisms exist when federal operations harm communities.”<br></p>
author: Mohammad Samra

title: Chicago's top cop stands by his officers interactions with ICE during Midway Blitz
summary: <p>Chicago police Supt. Larry Snelling is standing by his department’s actions during ramped-up immigration enforcement last year, telling residents his officers were “out there working to keep communities safe.”</p><p>Snelling joined the Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability for a “special hearing” Thursday to discuss his department's interactions with federal immigration agents.</p><p>Dozens of people attended, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/01/08/residents-voice-frustrations-with-chicago-police-interactions-during-immigration-raids-who-protects-us" target="_blank" ><u>some accusing Chicago police of illegally coordinating with immigration agents</u></a> during President Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation campaign.</p><p>A similar meeting back in January also was packed, but this time around those attending heard responses from Snelling directly, leading to some tense moments in the crowd.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> title: Venezuelan immigrant accused of killing Loyola freshman Sheridan Gorman now faces federal gun charge
summary: <p>Chicago’s top federal prosecutor said he’s taking “no chances”<b> </b>that Sheridan Gorman’s alleged killer will be released, filing an illegal gun possession charge<b> </b>Thursday<b> </b>against the Venezuelan immigrant already charged with the murder of the Loyola University Chicago freshman.</p><p>No federal court date has been scheduled for Jose Medina, 25,<b> </b>who was ordered detained Friday<b> </b>by a state court judge<b> </b>in connection with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/24/heres-what-to-know-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >Gorman’s slaying</a>. Medina’s attorney actually asked Cook County Circuit Court Judge D’Anthony Thedford<b> </b>to hold Medina in jail so he won’t be deported.</p><p>Now the feds have charged Medina with possessing<b> </b>a Smith & Wesson .40-caliber semiautomatic pistol while being unlawfully present in the United States, a charge carrying a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.</p><p>“Given the senseless, cold-blooded nature of the murder of a young student with a bright future ahead of her, the Chicago U.S. attorney’s office will take no chances that this illegal alien perpetrator will be released back into our community,” U.S. Attorney Andrew S. Boutros said in a statement.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fe0000" the gun turned out to be a high-probability match for the one used in Gorman’s slaying.</p><p>The federal complaint lays out how Medina was born in Venezuela and has “no lawful status in the United States.”<b> </b>It says a Border Patrol agent “encountered”<b> </b>Medina<b> </b>in the El Paso border sector on May 9, 2023. Medina was allegedly unable to provide a valid U.S. address but said he planned to reside in New Rochelle, New York.</p><p>Medina was released on his own recognizance on May 24, 2023, and was scheduled to appear for a hearing before an immigration judge in New York on Oct. 13, 2023, according to the complaint.</p><p>However, it says there “is no indication of any record of any further immigration related proceedings or adjustments in status.”</p><p>Gorman’s killing reignited the national debate over immigration and even drew the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" target="_blank" >attention of President Donald Trump</a>. Medina is accused of hiding at the end of a pier near Tobey Prinz Beach and shooting the 18-year-old Gorman<b> </b>in the back as she and her friends ran for cover.</p><p>Cook County Assistant Public Defender Julie Koehler has said that Medina <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/27/sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-jose-medina" target="_blank" >has a developmental disability</a> stemming from an earlier gunshot wound he suffered to his head during a robbery in Colombia. Medina had made his way to that country after fleeing violence in Venezuela, Koehler said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure He can’t read or write, Koehler said.</p><p>Medina wound up in Chicago in 2023 after reaching the U.S.-Mexico border in Texas and being detained there, according to Koehler. Although he asked to be deported back to Colombia, officials in Texas purportedly bused him to Chicago.</p><p>With no family here, Medina stayed in a migrant shelter and contracted tuberculosis that went undiagnosed, his attorney said. His mother eventually joined him here, and he was staying with her at an apartment building a block from where Gorman was killed.</p><p>Gorman’s family has said they “understand”<b> </b>the instinct for compassion.</p><p>“Every life has a story,” they said in a statement last week. “But we cannot lose sight of the simple, devastating truth at the center of all of this: Sheridan had a life too. title: Local officials warn of ICE arrests at domestic violence courthouse, decry feds violating state law
summary: <p>Federal immigration agents are violating Illinois law and making arrests at Chicago-area courthouses, several local officials alleged at a press conference Thursday.</p><p>The Cook County Public Defender’s office said since late February, federal immigration agents have been spotted entering the Domestic Violence Courthouse at 555 W. Harrison St., or waiting directly outside.</p><p>In at least two of those instances, someone was arrested, including that of a woman <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/groups/378158360786470/posts/1530031978932430/" target="_blank" ><u>followed out of the courthouse</u></a> and detained by federal agents March 10. The other occurred February 27, officials said. Still another person was detained on March 18 at a different location, the Maywood courthouse.</p><p>The press conference was held hours after federal agents returned to the courthouse with “the intent to take custody of a person who was scheduled to appear for a hearing today,” the Cook County Public Defender’s office said. Officials said they weren’t aware of any arrests being made Thursday, but noted they don’t always immediately know when someone is taken.</p><p></p><p>“Survivors should be able to walk into a courthouse without fear [that] doing the right thing will put a target on their backs,” State Rep. Graciela Guzmán <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/ICIRR/videos/1656661488801326" target="_blank" ><u>said at Thursday’s press conference</u></a>. “This is contempt for our laws, our courts and survivors.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fd0000" name="image-fd0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f02d21c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2Fe2%2F89870f11464797e4fab006a26450%2Ficepresser-260403-06.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/43d4b8f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2Fe2%2F89870f11464797e4fab006a26450%2Ficepresser-260403-06.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/14c5806/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2Fe2%2F89870f11464797e4fab006a26450%2Ficepresser-260403-06.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Sen. Guzman represents the 20th District." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/14c5806/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2Fe2%2F89870f11464797e4fab006a26450%2Ficepresser-260403-06.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d4ff143/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2Fe2%2F89870f11464797e4fab006a26450%2Ficepresser-260403-06.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/14c5806/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2Fe2%2F89870f11464797e4fab006a26450%2Ficepresser-260403-06.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>State Sen. Graciela Guzmán, D-Chicago, speaks about recent Immigration and Customs enforcement during a press conference at the Cook County Offices at 118 S. Clark St. in the Loop on Thursday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Immigrations and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker signed a law in December banning federal agents from conducting civil immigration enforcement at state courthouses after the Chief Judge’s office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/14/top-cook-county-judge-bars-civil-arrests-at-courthouses-citing-chilling-effect" >barred civil arrests at county courthouses</a> in October. Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle also signed an executive order <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/16/preckwinkle-issues-executive-order-to-create-ice-free-zones-in-cook-county" >prohibiting feds from staging on county property</a> as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/06/mayor-brandon-johnson-executive-order-city-owned-properties-ice-free-zones" >Chicago</a>, Evanston and others did the same.</p><p>Officials pointed to a pivot in federal immigration activity, away from neighborhoods where they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/12/ice-chicago-albany-park-tear-gas" >faced heavy resistance</a>, and to places like courthouses and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/23/ice-agents-ohare-airport-partial-government-shutdown" >airports</a> where it can be more difficult for communities to respond.</p><p>Sharlyn Grace, deputy public defender for policy at the Cook County Public Defender’s office, said reports of federal agents using county property to stage had fallen off since Preckwinkle’s order banning them from doing so, which she said was a good sign for the legislative tools officials did have.</p><p>However, the law they alleged federal agents were violating doesn't carry criminal penalties; it requires the person detained to file a civil lawsuit — something she admitted is already a challenge for those detained by the feds.</p><p>“It’s one of our only tools,” Grace said. “But it’s obviously limited by a person in immigration custody to access a lawyer.”</p><p>Maralea Negron, vice president of policy and impact at The Network: Advocating Against Domestic Violence, said having Border Patrol and ICE agents at courthouses would have a “chilling effect” on domestic violence survivors working with the justice system.</p><p>“Our society tells survivors to report to law enforcement and go to the courts, and yet when they do, they and their families can be taken,” Negron said. “The presence of ICE makes the decision to leave an abusive relationship or household even harder.”</p><div title: Felony case dropped against DePaul student accused of spitting on ICE agent at Chicago's O'Hare Airport
summary: <p>Cook County’s top prosecutor abruptly dropped a felony case against a DePaul University student accused of spitting on an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent over the weekend at O’Hare Airport.</p><p>In an arrest report, Chicago police said Brett Heier “intentionally and forcefully” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/01/ice-trump-depaul-spitting-chicago-ohare-crime" target="_blank" >spat on the ICE agent</a> Sunday while leaving Terminal 2 at O’Hare. Heier, 20, was charged with felony aggravated battery to a peace officer and was ordered released pending trial during his first court appearance Wednesday. </p><p>By Thursday evening, Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke had “personally reviewed the case and directed prosecutors to dismiss the charge,” according to a statement released by her office. The unusual move comes as O’Neill Burke faces mounting calls to investigate and prosecute immigration agents who carried out an aggressive deportation campaign in the Chicago area.</p><p>The statement didn't provide an explanation for dismissing the case, saying only that O'Neill Burke's office "continually evaluates evidence and reviews cases presented to us by law enforcement to ensure charging decisions are appropriate."</p><p>Heier's lawyer, Adam Sheppard, had insisted in an interview with the Sun-Times that the case was overblown. Sheppard argued Heier was only accused of spitting on the agent's shoe, and it may have been unintentional.</p><p>“It is comforting to know that the Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office will exercise proper prosecutorial discretion,” Sheppard said after the case was dropped.</p><p>The alleged spitting incident at O’Hare came a week after President Donald Trump announced he was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/23/ice-agents-ohare-airport-partial-government-shutdown" target="_blank" >sending ICE agents to airports</a> across the country to assist with security amid the fight over funding for the Department of Homeland Security.</p><p>The government shutdown resulting from that funding fight has led to long lines at airports and staffing issues among Transportation Security Administration agents, who went unpaid from mid-February until Trump signed an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/travel/2026/03/26/tsa-travel-airports-dhs-ice-ohare-federal-budget-congress-impasse-government-shutdown" target="_blank" >executive order giving them back-pay</a> last week.</p><p>Employees of other DHS agencies, including ICE and Customs and Border Protection, have continued to earn paychecks because they’re being funded by Trump’s domestic policy bill passed over the summer.</p><p>The shutdown was prompted by Democrats’ unanswered calls for reforms after two U.S. citizens were fatally shot during an immigration enforcement operation in Minnesota earlier this year.</p><p>O'Neill Burke has said she’s legally handcuffed when it comes to targeting the feds who carried out the earlier campaign in the Chicago area — even as legal efforts have been launched to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-cook-county-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor-oneill-burke-loevy" target="_blank" >install a special prosecutor</a> in her office to do just that.</p>
author: Sophie Sherry

title: DePaul student charged with spitting on ICE agent at O'Hare, but lawyer says felony case is overblown
summary: <p>A DePaul University student was charged with spitting on an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent working at O’Hare Airport amid a partial government shutdown prompted by calls to reform ICE.</p><p>Brett Heier, 20, "intentionally and forcefully" spat on the agent Sunday evening while leaving Terminal 2 at O’Hare, according to a Chicago police arrest report. Heier faces a felony charge of aggravated battery to a peace officer.</p><p>But his lawyer, Barry Sheppard, argued that his client is only accused of spitting on the agent's shoe, and it may have been unintentional. The arrest report notes that Heier was taking medication for an abscessed tooth.</p><p>"In the past, [ICE] seems to have made smaller incidents larger than life," Sheppard said in an interview, "and I feel this one was also blown out of proportion."</p><p>A spokesperson for ICE said its employees “are grappling with a 1,300% increase in assaults, a 3,200% increase in vehicle attacks and a staggering 8,000% uptick in death threats as they put their lives on the line to arrest murderers, rapists, pedophiles, and gang members.”</p><p>The ICE agent who was allegedly hit by the spit identified Heier’s photo in a lineup, along with a second agency official. Chicago cops arrested Heier Tuesday as he left his Lincoln Park apartment, and he was ordered released from custody during his first court hearing Wednesday. </p><p>The alleged spitting incident at O’Hare came a week after President Donald Trump announced he was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/23/ice-agents-ohare-airport-partial-government-shutdown" target="_blank" >sending ICE agents to airports</a> across the country to assist with security amid the fight over DHS funding.</p><p>The resulting government shutdown has led to long lines at airports and staffing issues among TSA agents, who went unpaid from mid-February until Trump signed an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/travel/2026/03/26/tsa-travel-airports-dhs-ice-ohare-federal-budget-congress-impasse-government-shutdown" target="_blank" >executive order giving them back pay</a> last week.</p><p>Employees of other DHS agencies, including ICE and Customs and Border Protection, have continued to earn paychecks because they’re being funded by Trump’s domestic policy bill passed over the summer.</p><p>The shutdown was prompted by Democrats’ unanswered calls for reforms after two U.S. citizens were fatally shot during an aggressive deportation campaign in Minnesota earlier this year.</p><p>Meantime, Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke has faced mounting calls to investigate and prosecute immigration agents who carried out a similar operation in the Chicago area. She has said she’s legally handcuffed when it comes to targeting the feds, even as legal efforts have been launched to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-cook-county-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor-oneill-burke-loevy" target="_blank" >install a special prosecutor</a> in her office to do just that.</p><p>A spokesperson for the state's attorney declined to comment on Heier’s case and the decision to charge him with a felony.</p><p>Heier’s attorney, Sheppard, said his client’s alleged actions fall under the "broad gamut of freedom of expression."</p><p>"He's a very good young man who does well in college, never had any type of arrest for anything before," Sheppard said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/23/ice-agents-ohare-airport-partial-government-shutdown" target="_blank" >ICE agents deployed at O’Hare as partial government shutdown continues to impact travelers</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/27/activists-protest-ice-agents-at-ohare-airport" target="_blank" >Activists protest ICE agents at O’Hare Airport</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-cook-county-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor-oneill-burke-loevy" target="_blank" >O’Neill Burke rejects bid for special prosecutor to target ICE, says it threatens to ‘thwart’ justice</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
author: Frank Main

title: Selective prosecution claims in 'Broadview Six' case the result of 'fevered paranoia,' feds say
summary: <p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago delivered a full-throated defense Monday<b> </b>of the conspiracy case leveled against the so-called “Broadview Six,”<b> </b>insisting that any claim of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >selective or vindictive prosecution</a> is “the product of fevered paranoia and delusional speculation.”</p><p>They mocked the notion that White House officials “had such an interest in local Illinois government”<b> </b>to pick “politically obscure figures”<b> </b>like Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh<b> </b>out of a crowd, “order their selective and vindictive prosecution, and blithely expect career prosecutors in Chicago to violate multiple ethical and legal standards.”</p><p>They also seemed to take such accusations personally, complaining that “the unavoidable conclusions to be drawn” are that officials in Chicago’s U.S. attorney’s office “have not only acted in bad faith but have committed prosecutorial misconduct.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/19/broadview-six-ice-trump-doj-justice-chicago-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >‘Broadview Six’ ICE protesters can see White House communications about their case — if they exist</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/16/chicago-broadview-six-kat-abughazaleh-midway-blitz-trump-ice" target="_blank" >Remaining ‘Broadview Six’ defendants want conspiracy charge tossed, argue protesting isn’t a crime</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Ultimately, prosecutors insisted that “there are no communications of any nature from, to, or with anyone” outside the U.S. attorney’s office regarding investigative or charging decisions in the case, aside from local FBI investigators.</p><p>“To be crystal clear, this specifically includes anyone in the White House and all components and offices of Main Justice,” Assistant U.S. Attorney William<b> </b>Hogan<b> </b>wrote in Monday’s 21-page court filing.</p><p>Hogan’s commentary came in the conspiracy case against a group of activists who protested outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility<b> </b>in Broadview last fall, during the Trump administration’s Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign.</p><p>The feds originally charged six of the activists but <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >dropped charges</a> against two. Still charged are former congressional candidate Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt and Andre Martin, a member of Abughazaleh’s campaign staff.</p><p>All four are involved in local Democratic politics.</p><p>The four are accused of a conspiracy to impede a federal agent. But defense attorneys have argued the indictment is another example of President Donald Trump’s administration using the Justice Department to target his “perceived political enemies.”</p><p>Defense attorneys have until Thursday to respond to Hogan’s court filing. Both sides are due back in U.S. District Judge April Perry’s courtroom<b> </b>April 7. The case is set for trial May 26.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4c0000" on the morning of Sept. 26 outside the ICE facility. The indictment alleges that, while a federal agent drove a vehicle toward the facility, the defendants and others surrounded it. Members of the larger crowd allegedly banged on the vehicle, pushed against it, scratched it and even etched the word “PIG” into it.</p><p>The crowd allegedly broke a side mirror and a rear windshield wiper and forced the agent “to drive at an extremely slow rate of speed.”</p><p>Defense attorneys say the agent did not wait for police to clear a path, did not identify himself and did not order the crowd to move aside.</p><p>Pushing back on the claims of selective prosecution, Hogan wrote Monday<b> </b>that videos "clearly show that most individuals who swarmed and impeded" the vehicle “could not be identified because they were wearing masks or other coverings that obscured their faces.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/16/chicago-broadview-six-kat-abughazaleh-midway-blitz-trump-ice" >Remaining ‘Broadview Six’ defendants want conspiracy charge tossed, argue protesting isn’t a crime</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But the feds “faced no comparable difficulty in identifying the original six defendants, each of whom was unmasked,” Hogan wrote. Some of them also made public statements confirming their presence at the facility during the incident, he added.</p><p>Even when the FBI positively identified others, prosecutors made the final call on who to charge “based on the strength of the evidence,”<b> </b>Hogan explained. They chose not to bring charges against a Chicago alderman, a “quasi-public figure who is well known”<b> </b>for protesting in Broadview, a prominent attorney and several others,<b> </b>the prosecutor added.</p><p>Hogan did not identify those individuals by name.</p><p>“Defendants have presented no evidence that individuals similarly situated to them were treated differently or that there was any improper purpose in the decision to charge them for the simple reason that there is no such evidence,” Hogan wrote.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/7b/73/8d13d19c425e81198b6bae06e586/usavrabbittcompelresponse.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

title: How we photographed ICE agents working at O'Hare Airport
summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Visual Journalist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/anthony-vazquez" target="_blank" >Anthony Vazquez</a>. Follow him on <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/avazquezphoto?utm_source=ig_web_button_share_sheet&igsh=ZDNlZDc0MzIxNw==" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3>What makes this photo important?</h3><p>This image captures the recent usage of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in the role of TSA officers. Seeing ICE and TSA personnel side-by-side is a visual representation of how the transition has taken effect. Many lawmakers have pushed back on the use of ICE agents in airports — as have travelers — due to the agency's history of racial profiling and the wrongful detention of U.S. citizens. For many, their presence represents a move toward more aggressive policing in public spaces, turning a routine travel gate into a source of fear and anxiety.</p><h3><b>How did you get the photo?</b></h3><p>This photograph was captured during a trip to O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, following news reports of ICE agents being deployed to airports due to TSA shortages. Initially, the deployment to O'Hare was unconfirmed, leading to a "goose chase" between different terminals to verify the reports. The situation changed as ICE officers made their presence more visible. Their masks potentially contributed to their reduced concealment, making documentation easier. This particular image was obtained at a Terminal 1 exit where the agents were openly present, standing guard alongside TSA workers.</p><h3>Technical details:</h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" title: Activists protest ICE agents at O'Hare Airport
summary: <p>Demonstrators gathered Friday evening at O’Hare International Airport to protest U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who have been called to assist with airport security amid a partial federal government shutdown.</p><p>ICE agents <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/23/ice-agents-ohare-airport-partial-government-shutdown" target="_blank" >had been seen</a> at O’Hare since Monday after President Donald Trump directed them to help the Transportation Security Administration’s operations at airports nationwide amid the Department of Homeland Security funding lapse.</p><p>No ICE agents were seen Friday in Terminal 1, where the couple dozen protesters gathered, or Terminal 2.</p><p>“ICE out of O’Hare, ICE out of everywhere,” protesters shouted.</p><p>After an hour of standing outside at the departures area, the protesters walked inside Terminal 1, chanting, “ICE out now.” Many travelers and airline workers laughed and took videos of the protesters. One man pointed in protesters’ faces and shouted, “Get out now.”</p><p>Once demonstrators returned to their initial staging area outside, Chicago police officers issued a dispersal order for unlawful assembly, which was triggered when the protesters went inside. Police vehicles then blocked access to the Terminal 1 drop off area. No arrests were reported.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d20000" class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Earlier Friday, Trump signed an executive action that will pay TSA workers, who have gone without pay for weeks since the DHS shutdown began Feb. 14.</p><p>The TSA has faced staffing shortages during the shutdown as Democrats and Republicans in Congress quarrel over funding for DHS, which oversees the TSA, ICE and the U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Democrats have refused to fund DHS without changes to immigration enforcement practices.</p><p>The shortage has resulted in long lines for security checkpoints at airports across the country. Travelers at O’Hare have experienced lengthy lines during busy travel weekends, however, many travelers have recently reported wait times of less than half an hour.</p><p>About 75 ICE agents were expected to be stationed at O’Hare, Mayor Brandon Johnson said earlier this week. Agents were monitoring exit lanes and checkpoints, not performing security screenings. Agents were not deployed to Midway.</p><p>Friday’s protesters pointed to the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign last fall in the Chicago area, “Operation Midway Blitz,” that brought an influx of ICE and CBP agents who roved the streets and made thousands of arrests. The operation involved a seemingly indiscriminate use of tear gas and other chemical irritants, and the fatal shooting of Silverio Villegas Gonzalez and the shooting of Marimar Martinez at the hands of federal agents.</p><p>“I don’t like what’s going on in our country with ICE agents terrorizing our communities,” said Melissa Espinoza, 45, who calmly stood along protest-designated fencing holding a sign reading, “ICE out now.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e80000" author: Kade Heather

title: Sheridan Gorman's suspected killer detained in Rogers Park ambush that stoked national immigration debate
summary: <p>In a case that has reignited a bitter national debate over immigration, and has even drawn <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" target="_blank" >the attention of President Donald Trump</a>, a Venezuelan immigrant accused of killing a Loyola University Chicago freshman in Rogers Park made his first court appearance Friday.</p><p>Jose Medina, 25, is accused of hiding at the end of a pier near Tobey Prinz Beach and shooting 18-year-old Sheridan Gorman in the back as she and her friends ran for cover on March 19. Medina appeared in court virtually Friday because he's being treated for tuberculosis in the Cook County Jail's medical unit.</p><p>In an unusual move, Medina's attorney asked Judge D'Anthony Thedford to hold Medina in the jail out of fear that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement would act on a detainer issued after the shooting. "We fear if he's released, ICE will detain him and release him to a third country," said Medina's attorney, Cook County Assistant Public Defender Julie Koehler.</p><div class="Enhancement" detained, as Cook County prosecutors had also requested.</p><p>During the hearing, Koehler disclosed that Medina has a developmental disability stemming from an earlier gunshot wound he suffered to his head during a robbery in Colombia. Medina had made his way to Colombia after fleeing violence in Venezuela, Koehler said.</p><p>Medina had to relearn how to walk and talk, and has an indentation on the top of his head. He can't read or write, Koehler said. </p><p>Medina wound up in Chicago in 2023 after reaching the U.S.-Mexico border in Texas and being detained there, Koehler said. Although he requested to be deported back to Colombia, officials in Texas bussed him to Chicago.</p><p>With no family here, Medina stayed in a migrant shelter and contracted tuberculosis that went undiagnosed, his attoreny said. His mother eventually joined him here, and he was staying with her at an apartment building a block from where Gorman was killed.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Colombia.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Cook County public defender’s office</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>An ambush attack</b></h3><p>In the hours before the shooting, Gorman and five friends had been hanging out at a dorm on campus, Assistant State's Attorney Mike Pekara said Friday. </p><p>A little after midnight, the group left to see the skyline, Pekara said. They took photos outside the dorm, then made their way to the lakefront and took more photos.</p><p>As two members of the group left to find a bathroom, Gorman and the others continued walking down the beach toward the pier, Pekara said. Gorman reached the end of the pier first and was startled to find Medina behind a structure, whispering that there was someone there, Pekara said.</p><p>Then, Medina jumped out wearing a black ski mask and holding a gun, Pekara said. The group started running away as Medina allegedly fired one round, striking Gorman in her upper back.</p><p>Gorman collapsed as the others "continued running for their lives," Pekara said. The others found shelter in the grass or behind a concrete barrier. They waited as Medina allegedly walked slowly back and forth on the pier. After Medina walked away, one of the friends ran back to find Gorman bleeding and unresponsive, Pekara said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> authorities arrived, they found two of Gorman's friends hiding and a single shell casing at the end of the pier, Pekara said. Gorman was taken to a hospital and pronounced dead.</p><p>Detectives eventually pinned the crime on Medina after analyzing video that led them to his apartment, Pekara said.</p><p>Video from the apartment building shows Medina left for the beach 20 minutes before the killing, Pekara said. The video allegedly shows him wearing a black ski mask and gloves, walking with a distinctive limp.</p><p>When police executed a search warrant on Medina's fourth-floor apartment, they found a gun wrapped in a ski mask near his bed and a leg brace with his name on it, Pekara said. Police also found clothes that match the ones seen in the video. </p><p>Medina was arrested during the search, Pekara said. He had an active warrant for an arrest in a 2023 shoplifting case. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >He is now charged</a> with first-degree murder, attempted murder and aggravated discharge of a firearm in Gorman's killing.</p><p>Medina's mother spoke with detectives and identified him in surveillance video, Pekara said. She said she remembered hearing him leave on the night of the shooting and noted that he walks with a limp from his gunshot injury.</p><p>Gorman's killing has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" target="_blank" >triggered widespread outrage</a>, especially among conservatives.</p><p>President Trump said Gorman’s killing was “devastating” and placed blame on the “open door policy” of his predecessor, Joe Biden. Other Republicans have directed their anger at Gov. JB Pritzker, Mayor Brandon Johnson and the sanctuary policies of the city and state.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >Man charged with murder of Loyola student Sheridan Gorman</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" target="_blank" >Sheridan Gorman’s killing puts Chicago back at the center of America’s bitter fight over immigration</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/24/heres-what-to-know-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >What to know about the killing of Sheridan Gorman</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
author: David Struett

title: State lawmakers advance bill to keep immigration detention centers out of communities like suburban Broadview
summary: <p>State lawmakers are taking steps to, in the future, keep immigration detention centers out of communities. </p><p>Under a bill that moved out of an Illinois House committee Wednesday, new immigration detention centers would be prohibited within 1,500 feet of schools, churches, day care centers, cemeteries, public parks, forest preserves, private residences and public housing. </p><p>Testifying in support of the legislation was House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch and Broadview Mayor Katrina Thompson, both of whom represent the Broadview area, where a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing center played a major role in Operation Midway Blitz last fall. The bill got broad support from Democrats, but was unanimously opposed by Republicans.</p><p>“This bill says something very simple and very reasonable: Detention facilities do not belong in the middle of our neighborhoods,” Welch said. “They should not be next to schools, they should not be next to day care centers, they should not sit beside parks, public housing, places of worship, or private homes like the Broadview detention center does.”</p><p>Welch noted that within 1,500 feet of the Broadview facility, there are two day care centers, a park, a place of worship and several private residences. The bill would not close the current Broadview center. </p><p>That facility became a flashpoint for anti-ICE protests during the deportation campaign. Six protesters, nicknamed<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/16/chicago-broadview-six-kat-abughazaleh-midway-blitz-trump-ice" > the Broadview Six, </a>were charged with conspiracy, a federal felony, following their participation in protests at the facility. Two of the six have had charges dropped. </p><p>Thompson testified about the financial strain of housing the Broadview center put on her community, which amounted to more than <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/broadview-mayor-demands-closure-of-ice-facility-reimbursement-of-village-costs-business-losses-police-fire-congress-trump-detention" target="_blank" ><u>$700,000</u></a>, according to village officials.</p><p>“For a small community like ours this is not just a number, that is a significant burden on our taxpayers, and yet there has been no reimbursement,” Thompson said.</p><p>Rep. Christopher Davidsmeyer, a Republican from Jacksonville, voted against the legislation, calling it just a "political bill." He expects it to be challenged in the courts if it passes.</p><p>“The reality is our laws have actually been pushing ICE’s actions in the directions they have been going,” Davidsmeyer said. “So if we would just work with them, things could happen peacefully and we wouldn't have this problem.”</p><p>The bill awaits votes in both the House and Senate. Several committee members asked to be added as co-sponsors to the bill. </p>
author: Matt Trunfio

title: Mayor Johnson unveils 'Abolish ICE' snowplow
summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson and city officials unveiled Wednesday the “Abolish ICE” snowplow, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/02/23/abolish-ice-among-winners-in-chicagos-you-name-a-snowplow-contest" target="_blank" >the winner of this year’s snowplow naming contest</a>, which drew a record number of submissions.</p><p>The mayor said the winning snowplow name is a message to the federal government that U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement isn’t welcome in Chicago.</p><p>But the unveiling in West Town came as Chicago has again become a focal point of America’s debate over immigration policies following last week’s fatal shooting of an 18-year-old college student.</p><p>Loyola University Chicago freshman Sheridan Gorman was shot and killed near the Rogers Park campus. The alleged gunman, Jose G. Medina, is a Venezuelan immigrant who had been taken into custody by U.S. Border Patrol in May 2023, released, then arrested again months later on shoplifting charges.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" >Sheridan Gorman’s killing puts Chicago back at the center of America’s bitter fight over immigration</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/24/heres-what-to-know-killing-sheridan-gorman" >What to know about the killing of Sheridan Gorman</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>One heckler at Wednesday’s event called out the mayor for unveiling the snowplow less than a week after Gorman’s death.</p><p>"You're making a joke out of Sheridan Gorman!" the heckler shouted. "Shame on you!"</p><p>“My condolences to the family of Sheridan. This is a terrible tragedy,” Johnson said. “And what I’ve said from the very beginning, I’m going to continue to use every single tool that’s available to me to protect the residents of the city of Chicago. And this tragedy is not going to deter us from our work. In fact, it’s going to challenge us all to double down on our efforts to ensure that we are protecting every single individual across neighborhoods.”</p><p>The fourth annual “You Name a Snowplow” contest returned in December and yielded 13,300 submissions. The slogan “Abolish ICE,” taking aim at the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, was submitted around 9,300 times, or about 70% of entries.</p><p>The flood of “Abolish ICE” entries followed several tense months in Chicago during which federal immigration agents caravanned around the city making arrests and deploying tear gas and other chemical irritants at protesters. Federal agents fatally shot one man, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/15/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-fatally-shot-by-ice-agents-touched-the-lives-of-so-many-loved-ones-say" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas Gonzalez</a>, and wounded a woman, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a>, in separate incidents.</p><p>Protests occurred regularly around the city and at the ICE processing facility in suburban Broadview.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/23/ice-agents-ohare-airport-partial-government-shutdown" target="_blank" >ICE agents were also deployed</a> to airports across the country, including to O'Hare Airport, on Monday amid a partial government shutdown that has left TSA officers working without pay for weeks.</p><p>“This name derives from our city’s legacy of standing up for justice, dignity and the rights of all people no matter where they come from,” Johnson said. “I want to take this moment to reiterate that Chicago does not want ICE on our streets, in our airports nor in our city. Chicago believes in abolishing ICE.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Zubaer Khan</i></p>
author: Kade Heather

title: What to know about the killing of Sheridan Gorman

She was a member of the campus Christian organization Cru and was studying business.</p><p><a class="Link" She made people feel valued. Whether it was her friends, her family, or someone she had just met, Sheridan had a way of leaving people better than she found them.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/support-for-the-gorman-family-cz6ns" target="_blank" >A fundraiser is gathering donations</a> for Gorman’s memorial and a scholarship in her honor. Over $150,000 was raised as of Tuesday.</p><h3>What happened to her? </h3><p>Gorman and her friends took an early morning stroll around 1:30 a.m. on March 19 to the pier at Tobey Prinz Beach — just north of the Rogers Park campus. They were hoping to capture photos of the city skyline and potentially the Northern Lights, her parents said in a statement.</p><p>Gorman was the first to reach the end of the pier when she spotted a masked gunman. He fired a single shot as Gorman and her friends fled, <a class="Link" </figure> </div> </div><p>The friends ran for cover when the shot rang out. But then they saw Gorman on the ground and went to her aid. She had been shot in the back, prosecutors said — not in the head as police initially reported. She was pronounced dead at the scene, according to authorities.</p><p>One of Gorman’s friends who witnessed the shooting told the Sun-Times that “it didn’t seem like it was intentionally targeted toward any of us.”</p><p>“It seemed like he was there for a reason, and we were just [in the] wrong place, wrong time. I’m guessing, because there was not another shot after that. It was just one,” the friend said.</p><h3>Who is the suspect? </h3><p>Jose Medina, 25, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >was arrested and charged in Gorman’s murder</a>. He faces charges of first-degree murder, attempted murder and aggravated discharge of a firearm.</p><p>He has yet to make his first appearance in court because he is currently hospitalized with tuberculosis. A full detention hearing was postponed until Friday, but <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/23/chicago-crime-trump-sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-shooting-deportation-immigration " target="_blank" >prosecutors provided a brief accounting</a> of the shooting in court on Monday.</p><p>Video captured Medina walking from the beach into a building in the 6800 block of North Sheridan Road, according to an arrest report. He wore all black clothing and a mask and had a “distinct gait.”</p><p>Police recovered black clothing and a .40 caliber handgun inside Medina’s apartment, prosecutors said. The gun matched the shell casing found at the shooting scene.</p><p>The arrest report shows police worked closely with U.S. Customs and Border Protection during the investigation. CBP used facial recognition to identify the man in the video as Medina, according to the report.</p><p>Records show Medina was born in Venezuela and at one point lived in a temporary migrant shelter at the Leone Beach Park Field House.</p><p>U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement issued an arrest detainer on March 22 naming Medina before police announced the charges. The Department of Homeland Security claims Medina entered the U.S. illegally. </p><p>Chicago police have not commented on his immigration status. Prosecutors also did not share that information in court Monday.</p><p>In May 2023, federal officials say he came into contact with Border Patrol agents and was released.</p><p>About a month later, he faced a single misdemeanor charge for shoplifting $132.50 of merchandise from the State Street Macy’s in June 2023. A judge issued a warrant for him in that case after he failed to appear for a court date. Records show the outstanding warrant is still active.</p><h3>How has Gorman’s death become politicized? </h3><p>President Donald Trump and his administration have used Gorman’s death to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/23/chicago-crime-trump-sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-shooting-deportation-immigration" target="_blank" >justify his push for mass deportations</a>.</p><p>Acting Assistant DHS Secretary Lauren Bis claimed in a statement Gorman was “failed by open border policies and sanctuary politicians.”</p><p>This isn't the first time the Trump administration has used a young woman's death to make the case that undocumented immigrants put Americans in danger. However, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/23/chicago-crime-trump-sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-shooting-deportation-immigration" target="_blank" >numerous studies have found</a> that immigrants without legal status are less likely to commit serious crimes than U.S.-born citizens.</p><p>The killing of Laken Riley, a nursing student in Georgia who was fatally attacked in 2024 by an immigrant, spurred federal legislation that mandates detention of undocumented immigrants accused of theft, burglary, assaulting a law enforcement officer and any crime that causes death or serious injury.</p><p>Operation Midway Blitz was dedicated to Katie Abraham, an Illinois native killed in 2025 by a drunken driver who allegedly lacked legal status. Notably, Abraham's mother <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2025/10/21/opinion-katie-abraham-operation-midway-blitz/" target="_blank" >wrote an op-ed</a> last fall decrying the administration's use of her daughter's name in immigration enforcement operations.</p><p>“Sheridan Gorman’s life was allegedly taken from her at the hands of a criminal alien shielded by the anti-American sanctuary policies of the city of Chicago and the state of Illinois,” U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said on social media Monday.</p><p>Legislation signed by former Illinois Gov. Bruce Rauner, a Republican, limits cooperation between local police and federal immigration authorities. The Illinois TRUST Act generally bars police from sharing information with immigration agents or handing over people in custody unless a federal criminal warrant is issued.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker issued a response saying, “Violent crime has no place in our streets.”</p><p>“We expect the alleged perpetrator to be held accountable to the fullest extent of the law,” Pritzker said in a statement. “The Trump Administration needs to stop politicizing heinous tragedies and instead focus on real solutions, like reinstating federal funds to prevent violence that support our public safety efforts.”</p><p>Panas in Chicago, a group that works with Venezuelan migrants, <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/panasenchicago" target="_blank" >said in a statement</a> the organization stands with Gorman’s family.</p><p>“Violence does not represent us,” the statement reads. “The Venezuelan community is made up of hardworking individuals with values, faith and a genuine commitment to contributing positively to the society that has welcomed us. We categorically reject any act of violence, regardless of who commits it. One individual’s actions, no matter how serious, do not define an entire community.”</p><h3><b>What’s next in the case? </b></h3><p>Medina, who remains hospitalized with tuberculosis, is scheduled to make his first full court appearance on Friday for a pretrial detention hearing. Judge Luciano Panici ordered he remain in custody pending the full hearing.</p><p>A community vigil and a private service will be held for Gorman on March 28 in Yorktown, New York.</p>
author: Sun-Times staff

title: Broadview mayor demands closure of ICE facility, reimbursement of village, business losses
summary: <p>The mayor of west suburban Broadview is calling on the federal government to shut down a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/01/broadview-immigration-processing-center-detention-ice-dhs" target="_blank" ><u>de facto immigration detention cente</u></a><u>r</u> that was the epicenter of protests — and violent responses from federal agents — that engulfed the small village last fall.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2025/10/04/broadview-mayor-katrina-thompson-ice-detention-center-arrests-kristi-noem-gregory-bovino" target="_blank" ><u>Mayor Katrina Thompson</u></a> is also asking the feds for a more than $700,000 reimbursement to make up for operational costs incurred by the village and economic losses suffered by two businesses adjacent to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility during Operation Midway Blitz, the intense deportation campaign that peaked from September through November.</p><p>She made the requests during a visit to Washington, D.C., earlier this month and in a letter to several members of the Illinois congressional delegation.</p><p>“Broadview did not ask for this operation, and our residents, our police officers, our firefighters, our business owners should not be the ones paying for it,” Thompson was quoted as saying in a news release. “I advocated for federal reimbursement for communities like ours impacted by ICE operations, emphasizing that local taxpayers should not bear the cost of federal responsibilities. I also pushed for the closure of the Broadview ICE Processing Center, centering dignity, safety, and a stronger vision for our community.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Mayor Katrina Thompson is looking to push Broadview past the trouble surrounding the ICE facility in the western suburb.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The municipal costs associated with responding to activity around the ICE facility amounted to $361,536, according to Broadview officials.</p><p>Records obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times through a freedom of information request show $71,185 of that sum was paid as police overtime, with more than $3,000 for additional personal protective equipment for officers. The village spent about $41,000 on legal costs, including for a federal lawsuit to remove a fence erected around the ICE facility. Ambulance transfers from the ICE facility’s address cost another nearly $250,000. And overtime for fire and ambulance personnel cost about $12,100.</p><p>Even before the requested federal reimbursement, it was still unclear whether the village would otherwise recoup any of that money, such as EMT transports that might be paid through Medicaid insurance.</p><p>Broadview officials also noted $353,813 in losses for two local businesses within two blocks of the ICE facility: Reynolds Advanced Materials and Wagner Brass Foundry, Inc.</p><p>The turmoil that roiled the village of about 8,000 residents in the fall spilled onto the front lawns and backyards of many neighbors. Hundreds of people showed up for near daily protests outside the facility where the vast majority of immigrants arrested during Operation Midway Blitz were taken for processing before being moved to detention facilities in the Midwest. Conditions described by detainees and advocates as “inhumane” festered in the overcrowded building, where people slept on floors with limited access to food or water.</p><p>Demonstrators, including clergy, were met with force from federal agents with ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection who often chased protesters through neighborhoods and shot rubber bullets and tear gas into the crowds.</p><p>In her letter to lawmakers, Thompson asked for help to close the facility and transfer its ownership from the federal government to the village for redevelopment as a museum. The “Broadview Justice Corridor,” as she called the project, would turn the ICE facility into a “national center dedicated to immigration history, civil rights education, civic leadership, and cultural tourism.</p><p>“This transformation would convert a site associated with fear, protest, and division into one that promotes education, reconciliation, and national dialogue,” Thompson wrote in the letter, estimating the proposal would draw up to 250,000 visitors annually and generate up to $31 million in economic activity.</p><p>Thompson’s appeal to the two senators and six representatives, all Democrats, is unlikely to sway President Donald Trump’s hard-line administration, which has looked to open new immigration detention centers in the past year rather than close any ICE facilities. Some of the lawmakers who received Thompson’s appeal were criticized by administration officials and denied entry to the Broadview facility last year as they sought to inspect the conditions.</p>
