title: O'Neill Burke rejects bid for special prosecutor to target ICE, says it threatens to 'thwart' justice
summary: <p>Cook County's top prosecutor argued Tuesday that a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-cook-county-oneill-burke-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor" target="_blank" >bid to name a special prosecutor</a> to investigate the federal agents behind last fall’s Operation Midway Blitz amounts to a “frivolous”<b> </b>and “heavy handed”<b> </b>attempt to usurp her authority — and could come at a cost.</p><p>State’s Attorney Eileen<b> </b>O’Neill Burke<b> </b>denied that any conflict exists to warrant the move. She said she’s not intimidated by “vague”<b> </b>threats of political retaliation. And she said a broad coalition’s argument to the contrary actually threatens to “thwart”<b> </b>justice.</p><p>“Acting outside the bounds of the law comes with a price,” O’Neill Burke argued. “And that price here would be compromising the prosecution’s ability to obtain justice for victims and the community.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-cook-county-oneill-burke-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor" >Seeking special prosecutor to target ICE, coalition says O’Neill Burke turned ‘blind eye’ to feds’ violence</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The commentary came in a 24-page response to the high-profile bid<b> </b>for a special prosecutor, launched earlier this month<b> </b>by a coalition of more than 200 elected officials, clergy, journalists and attorneys. They say O’Neill Burke has turned a “blind eye”<b> </b>to myriad crimes committed by federal agents during the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation blitz last fall.</p><p>The alleged crimes include murder, assault, perjury and even conspiracy. The coalition’s March 12 petition<b> </b>seeking a special prosecutor prominently cited the September killing of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/15/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-fatally-shot-by-ice-agents-touched-the-lives-of-so-many-loved-ones-say" target="_blank" >Silverio<b> </b>Villegas<b> </b>Gonzalez</a><b> </b>and the October<b> </b>shooting of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a>, both at the hands of federal agents.</p><p>Now O’Neill Burke has submitted the most substantive response to her critics to date. She insisted any investigation must be conducted by law enforcement, but also noted that any prosecutor “should be loath to provide information on any ongoing investigation.”</p><p>“Petitioners are claiming that the state’s attorney has an actual conflict because she is not abdicating her prosecutorial discretion to elected officials and the public or succumbing to political pressure,” she argued in her filing.</p><p>O’Neill Burke again pointed to a 2017 <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoiscourts.gov/resources/bb31d7b0-e90c-4843-8486-c740ae2624ef/file" target="_blank" >Illinois Supreme Court decision</a> she says limits her ability to investigate the agents. But coalition attorney Steve Art insisted that every special prosecutor “takes on the role of an elected state’s attorney and investigates and prosecutes” a crime.</p><p>Art said O’Neill Burke’s argument is “exactly”<b> </b>why a special prosecutor is needed. The coalition he represents has been “asking for justice for months,”<b> </b>he said.</p><p>“Instead of getting any commitment to do justice — to investigate, to prosecute — all we get from the state’s attorney is legal obstacles,” Art told reporters Tuesday.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/02/06/how-can-chicagos-top-prosecutor-hold-ice-accountable" >How can Chicago’s top prosecutor hold ICE accountable?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>O’Neill Burke’s deputies filed her response to the petition during a brief hearing Tuesday before Cook County Circuit Judge Erica<b> </b>Reddick, the presiding judge of the criminal division. Lawyers are due back April 10<b> </b>in Reddick’s courtroom<b> </b>at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse.</p><p>The coalition includes the Chicago News Guild, which represents journalists at the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>Prosecuting federal agents in state court would require <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/08/can-state-officials-prosecute-the-feds-calls-grow-after-minneapolis-shooting" target="_blank" >showing they acted unreasonably</a> while fulfilling their duties. Meanwhile, prosecutors like O’Neill Burke are entrusted with discretion to choose which cases to pursue. The coalition argued O’Neill Burke’s impartiality “has been irrevocably tainted” by her failure to respond to public demands<b> </b>for an investigation, though.</p><p>In her filing Tuesday, O’Neill Burke repeatedly cited the Illinois Supreme Court ruling addressing the power of a state’s attorney to investigate alleged crimes.</p><p>The court found the duty is “limited to circumstances where other law enforcement agencies inadequately deal with such investigation … or where a law enforcement agency asks the state’s attorney for assistance.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" >Cook County’s top prosecutor outlines plan to charge ICE agents with crimes</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“Petitioners make no allegation that the state’s attorney has been presented with any credible evidence from law enforcement which she refused to charge,” O’Neill Burke wrote Tuesday, “but instead fault her with not investigating criminal conduct, where they have not established it is her duty to investigate.”</p><p>She said the coalition failed to find any “specific personal interest”<b> </b>creating a conflict. She rejected the idea that she’s susceptible to intimidation by President Donald Trump’s Justice Department. And in any event, she said no specific threat of retaliation has been made.</p><p>“It is common for people to threaten the state’s attorney or her assistants,” O’Neill Burke wrote, “and those threats generally do not engender any concern from outside parties or prompt the filing of a petition to appoint a special prosecutor.”</p><p>O’Neill Burke criticized the coalition for “boldly”<b> </b>seeking input in the process of selecting a special prosecutor. She also took a shot at the law firm leading the charge, Loevy and Loevy, for its handling of separate litigation in federal court last fall.</p><p>The firm helped <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >secure an order</a> from U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis restricting the feds’ use of force during Midway Blitz. But later, after the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals signaled the feds<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/19/federal-appeals-court-halts-ruling-that-curbed-use-of-force-during-immigration-campaign" target="_blank" >were likely to prevail</a> in the end, the firm <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/02/lawyers-who-secured-bovino-testimony-body-cam-video-move-to-end-case-that-challenged-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >sought to dismiss the case</a> voluntarily.</p><p>The appeals court formally vacated Ellis’ order<b> </b>earlier this month, citing in part the voluntary dismissal.</p><p>“These times call for serious people,” O’Neill Burke wrote Tuesday. “Not those who cut and run ‘at the first sign of trouble.’”</p><p><i>Neither the reporter nor editors who worked on this story — including some represented by the News Guild — have been involved in the litigation described in this article.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/70/0f/0d9f739b4ad8909f116f7deb173c/eobresponse.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

All the while she had her baby in tow.</p><p><b>Touring while parenting</b>: Mäkelä is ramping up events with Chicago’s orchestra as he prepares to take the podium in 2027. title: ICE agents spotted at O’Hare Airport as partial government shutdown continues to impact travelers
summary: <p>U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers were present at O'Hare International Airport Monday, after the Trump administration said agents would be deployed to airports nationwide to help amid the ongoing partial government shutdown.</p><p>At least three agents in ICE gear were seen at Terminal 3 around 10 a.m. Monday morning.</p><p>A day after saying he would use immigration officers for <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/government-shutdown-tsa-workers-920577c153ffd1877f59dfb8f8efed39" target="_blank" ><u>airport security</u></a> starting Monday unless Democrats agreed on a bill to fund the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/us-department-of-homeland-security" target="_blank" ><u>Department of Homeland Security</u></a>, Trump made clear Sunday that he was going ahead with the plan to assist the Transportation Security Administration.</p><p>O’Hare was among 13 airports included in a list of where ICE agents would be present to assist, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/us/live-news/tsa-wait-times-ice-airports-03-23-26?post-id=cmn37qf65000q3b6rfo32wpep" target="_blank" >according to CNN</a>. Department of Homeland Security acting assistant secretary Lauren Bis said in a statement, “For operational security reasons, we are not going to confirm the locations of our officers," but flagged nine major airports, including Baltimore/Washington International Airport in Maryland and John F. Kennedy Airport International in New York as having high TSA worker callout rates on Sunday. O'Hare and Midway Airports were not on that list.</p><p>Luke Hoover and Mary Dickey, of North Center, were on their way to New Zealand for their honeymoon and got to O'Hare three hours early for their flight after bracing for possible delays stemming from the partial government shutdown. </p><p>"It gives us pause, [we're] not a big fan of it," Hoover said of ICE agents at O'Hare. "We figured with that plus TSA just being a bit of a mess lately, we'd get here early and ready to go." </p><p>"Just [the] TSA process alone, having people who aren’t trained in the process trying to, you know, expedite the process, just doesn’t make sense to me," Dickey added. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a "They're doing violent things to U.S. citizens and citizens from other countries, so I don’t think it's proper [for them] to be here." </p><p>White House border czar Tom Homan said during Sunday news show interviews that ICE's increased role at airports was subject to discussions with the leadership of the agency and the TSA “to find out where we can fit in.” Immigration officers, as an example, could cover exits currently monitored by TSA agents, freeing them to work screening lines, or have ICE agents check identification before people enter screenings areas.</p><p>During an appearance on Chris Cuomo’s SiriusXM show Monday, Homan expanded on how ICE agents will work with airport security and predicted that agents will be met with protesters.</p><p>"We're going to first send out to the biggest airports with the biggest wait lines. Homan told the program’s executive producer, Alexandra “Dusty” Cohen.</p><p>When asked if that meant he was already preparing for protests, Homan responded, "I'm sure there will be. class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>No ICE agents were spotted at Midway, but some travelers still felt impacted.</p><p>Anayeli Castro, who was waiting for her husband by the security check point with her two young kids, had heard online that they should arrive at least four hours early. She tried checking the TSA app to see how long the security line was but the app was not updating the wait time.</p><p>“I'm here three hours before, luckily the lines are not long right now,” Castro said. “We normally arrive two hours early but I when heard you have to be here 4 to 5 hours early, I was freaking out.”</p><p>She also saw on social media that ICE agents could be deployed to Chicago airports.</p><p>“They're ICE agents. It's different from TSA, so it does kind of freak you out a little bit," Castro said. “I am an immigrant, so it's scary but it seems pretty calm right now.”</p><p>Lori Houzer found a place to sit at Midway Airport while she waited to check her bags for her flight to Canada. She said she followed recommended instructions to arrive three to four hours beforehand but despite the early arrival there are no staff to check in passengers.</p><p>“I would have arrived max two hours early if I'm checking luggage, which is more than enough time, sometimes an hour and a half,” she said. “Now it's at least two hours more, and that's if things go well,” she said.</p><p>Houzer said she kept up with the news and knew TSA agents were not getting paid due to the government shutdown.</p><p>“People should get paid because not only is it incorrect to ask people who already aren't earning very much money to get no money, but also what is their motivation for doing their job really well?” she said. “It's a security job. I would like people to take it seriously.”</p><p>She isn’t worried about ICE agents being at airports, but she does think it’s a bad use of funds.</p><p>“They're gonna pay ICE but they're not gonna pay regular people?” she questioned. “I'm also Canadian. I don't really understand it very well.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/22/union-tsa-workers-push-back-demand-pay-after-trump-admin-deploys-ice-agents-in-airports-monday" target="_blank" >TSA union officials raised concerns</a> over passenger security with ICE agents present.</p><p>“Our members at TSA have been showing up every day, without a paycheck, because they believe in the mission of keeping the flying public safe,” Everett Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, said in a statement Sunday. “They deserve to be paid, not replaced by untrained, armed agents who have shown how dangerous they can be.”</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p><p><i>Contributing Violet Miller</i></p>

title: Venezuelan migrant charged with murder of Loyola student Sheridan Gorman
summary: <p>A Venezuelan migrant has been charged with the murder of Loyola University Chicago student Sheridan Gorman, police announced Sunday, prompting outrage from Trump administration officials who branded her killing as the result of sanctuary policies in Illinois. </p><p>Jose Medina, 25, faces charges of first-degree murder, attempted murder and aggravated discharge of a firearm for the March 19 attack near a pier at Tobey Prinz Beach, according to Chicago police. </p><p>Federal immigration authorities said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement issued an arrest detainer naming Medina hours before police announced the charges. </p><p>The Department of Homeland Security said Medina was taken into custody by the U.S. Border Patrol in May 2023, released and then taken into custody again two months later for shoplifting. He was charged with misdemeanor retail theft in that case, accused of stealing $132.50 of merchandise from the State Street Macy's, county court records show. An outstanding warrant from that case is active.</p><p>Records show Medina was born in Venezuela and at one point lived in a temporary migrant shelter at the Leone Beach Park Field House, which closed in 2024. He was among thousands of migrants who arrived in Chicago, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2024/02/15/busing-migrants-chicago-texas-origins-start-donald-trump-tucker-carlson-ted-cruz" >many of them bused to the city by GOP Texas Gov. Greg Abbott</a> in protest of former President Joe Biden's border policies. </p><p>Acting Assistant DHS Secretary Lauren Bis claimed in a statement that Gorman was "failed by open border policies and sanctuary politicians" and urged Gov. JB Pritzker to not release Medina, who was scheduled to make his first court appearance Monday. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure </div><p>Pritzker's office did not have any immediate comment. </p><p>Legislation signed by Republican former Illinois Gov. Bruce Rauner limits cooperation between local police and federal immigration authorities. The Illinois TRUST Act generally bars police from sharing information with immigration agents or handing over people in custody unless a federal criminal warrant is issued, a policy long denigrated by President Donald Trump and other conservative critics.</p><p>Gorman, 18, and her friends took an early morning stroll Thursday just north of the Rogers Park campus, hoping to capture some photos with a view of the skyline and potentially the Northern Lights, her family said in a statement.</p><p>When they arrived, a masked gunman “emerged from the shadows” and fired a single shot as they fled, according to a Chicago police report. One of Gorman’s friends <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/20/chicago-loyola-sheridan-gorman-rogers-park-crime-shooting-murder" target="_blank" ><u>who witnessed the shooting</u></a> told the Chicago Sun-Times that “it didn’t seem like it was intentionally targeted toward any of us.”</p><p>The friends ran in different directions when the shot was fired, but returned when they saw Gorman on the ground. She had been shot in her torso and was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/19/woman-18-shot-to-death-in-predawn-rogers-park-attack" target="_blank" ><u>pronounced dead at the scene</u></a>, officials said.</p><p>In a statement, Gorman's family said they were "gravely disappointed by the policies and failures that allowed this individual to remain in a position to commit this crime. </p><p>"When systems fail — whether through release decisions, lack of coordination, or unwillingness to act — the consequences are not abstract. They are real. And in our case, they are permanent," Gorman's family said. “This case must be prosecuted to the fullest extent of both state and federal law. There can be no gaps, no shortcuts, and no second chances that put others at risk. Accountability must be complete.”</p><p>The family insisted "we will not allow this to be dismissed as ‘wrong place, wrong time.’ This was not random misfortune. This was a violent and preventable act.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/20/chicago-loyola-sheridan-gorman-rogers-park-crime-shooting-murder" >Friend of slain Loyola student Sheridan Gorman says Rogers Park shooting didn’t feel ‘targeted’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/21/police-questioning-person-of-interest-in-fatal-shooting-of-18-year-old-loyola-student" >Police questioning person of interest in fatal shooting of 18-year-old Loyola student</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/19/woman-18-shot-to-death-in-predawn-rogers-park-attack" >Loyola University student, 18, shot to death in predawn attack at Rogers Park beach</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Judge rules Broadview protest curfew violates First Amendment
summary: <p>A federal Judge on Sunday struck down the village of Broadview’s curfew on protests, ruling that restrictions set by suburban leaders have violated demonstrators' First Amendments rights. </p><p>Chicago attorney Robert Held filed for a preliminary injunction <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/11/13/lawyer-seeking-preliminary-injunction-in-lawsuit-against-broadview-over-protest-hours-appears-outside-ice-facility" >last fall</a> as part of a federal lawsuit against Broadview to overturn Mayor Katrina Thompson’s executive order establishing time limits and designated areas for protests outside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Edmond Chang granted the preliminary injunction, writing in his decision that Broadview’s “current restrictions cannot stand under the First Amendment.”</p><p>Held called the ruling a “heartwarming victory.”</p><p>“The judge looked at the facts and the law and slapped down mayor,” Held told the Sun-Times. “This is a victory not just for the protesters, but anyone in this country who cares about the First Amendment and Constitution.”</p><p>The ICE property became the site <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/11/14/scuffles-erupt-during-broadview-protest-several-arrested" >for major protests</a> against “Operation Midway Blitz,” the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign in Chicago and its suburbs last year.</p><p>In response, Thompson issued several executive orders restricting where and when people can protest at the facility, which included establishing “free speech zones” and a daily curfew for demonstrations from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.</p><p>Held filed the federal complaint in October against Thompson and Broadview Chief of Police Thomas Mills in an effort to overturn the village’s protest restrictions.</p><p>In granting the preliminary injunction, Chang said the ongoing daily limits on protests “fail to survive First Amendment scrutiny.” But the village is allowed to keep the protest zones and enact “more specific limits for specific protests on specific days.”</p><p>A Broadview spokesperson did not immediately respond a request for comment.</p><p><i>Contributing: Violet Miller</i> </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/6d/90/bf9520534073a8b9fdcd01ee8bdc/broadviewpiopinion.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

title: 'Broadview Six' ICE protesters can see White House communications about their case — if they exist
summary: <p>If the White House encouraged<b> </b>Chicago’s U.S. attorney's office in writing to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >bring a conspiracy<b> </b>indictment</a> against six<b> </b>immigration protesters last fall, defense attorneys should be allowed to see it, a prosecutor agreed Thursday.</p><p>But Assistant U.S. Attorney William<b> </b>Hogan<b> </b>said he didn’t expect to find anything related to the case against the so-called “Broadview Six.” Hogan made the comment while speaking to U.S. District Judge<b> </b>April Perry about recent defense motions in the case.</p><p>“To my knowledge — I’m not saying that I know for sure — but my understanding is there is no such communication,” Hogan said. “Certainly, [there] was none before the indictment.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/16/chicago-broadview-six-kat-abughazaleh-midway-blitz-trump-ice" >Remaining ‘Broadview Six’ defendants want conspiracy charge tossed, argue protesting isn’t a crime</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Hogan also confirmed for the judge that prosecutors still expect to take four of the original six defendants to trial. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >The feds last week dropped charges</a> against musician<b> </b>Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh<b> </b>and former Cook County Board candidate Catherine “Cat” Sharp.</p><p>Still charged are<b> </b>former congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael<b> </b>Rabbitt and Andre Martin,<b> </b>a member of Abughazaleh’s campaign staff. They’re all set for trial May 26.</p><p>Straw was the only defendant to attend Thursday’s hearing.<b> </b>Each of the four remaining defendants are involved in local Democratic politics.<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/us-house-illinois-9th-congressional-district-primary-results" target="_blank" >Abughazaleh placed second</a> in Tuesday’s primary for the Democratic nomination for Illinois’ 9th Congressional District seat, won by Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Thursday, March 19, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The four are accused of a conspiracy to impede a federal agent. The charges revolve around events on the morning of Sept. 26 outside the<b> </b>U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview.</p><p>An indictment alleges that, while a federal agent drove a vehicle toward the ICE facility, the defendants and others surrounded it. Members of the larger crowd allegedly banged on the vehicle, pushed against it, scratched it and even etched the word “PIG” into it.</p><p>The crowd allegedly broke a side mirror and a rear windshield wiper and forced the agent “to drive at an extremely slow rate of speed.”</p><p>However, video also shows that, after the agent drove the vehicle into the crowd, Abughazaleh grabbed a bullhorn and told fellow protesters, “that’s private property back there, come back here now.”</p><p>Defense attorneys say the agent did not wait for police to clear a path, did not identify himself and did not order the crowd to move aside.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" >Broadview 4? Feds drop conspiracy charges against 2 ICE protesters, including Dem who ended campaign</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Perry on Thursday asked Hogan<b> </b>to confirm that U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office received no communication from the White House encouraging the prosecution. Defense attorneys sought that and other records in a motion filed late last week. Perry spent much of Thursday’s hearing walking both sides through each defense request.</p><p>Along the way, Hogan told Perry<b> </b>the person who scratched the word “PIG”<b> </b>into the agent’s vehicle “was not identified.”<b> </b>The prosecutor also agreed that, if any internal communication exists among the feds suggesting people should be prosecuted for their political beliefs, that should likely be turned over to the defense.</p><p>Finally, the lawyers discussed a <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/19/us/politics/justice-dept-prosecute-protesters.html?unlocked_article_code=1.UVA.M2DW.BUUcCgAY4KzX&smid=url-share" target="_blank" >New York Times article</a> published Thursday<b> </b>about criminal charges brought nationally against protesters as a result of President Donald Trump’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/09/countering-domestic-terrorism-and-organized-political-violence/" target="_blank" >National Security Presidential Memorandum 7</a>. Known as NSPM-7, it addresses “domestic terrorism and organized political violence” and cites the assassination of Charlie Kirk.</p><p>Trump issued the memo<b> </b>Sept. 25, one day before the incident at Broadview that led to the conspiracy indictment against the Chicago protesters.</p><p>Hogan told the judge he was unaware of the memo until the New York Times article was emailed to him by defense attorneys<b> </b>about two hours before Thursday’s hearing.</p><p>“We’ll look into that,” he said.</p>
author: Jon Seidel

title: Pritzker taunts Bovino amid reports of Border Patrol chief’s retirement: 'No one is above the law'
summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker on Monday celebrated the reported retirement of U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino, who led President Donald Trump’s aggressive — and at times deadly — deportation campaigns in Chicago and other cities.</p><p>“Greg Bovino won’t just get to walk away — he will be held accountable and responsible for the damage he’s done to our nation,” Pritzker said on the social media platform X. “We won’t forget, and neither should you. No one is above the law.”</p><p>Bovino reportedly told <a class="Link" href="“The greatest honor of my entire life was to work alongside Border Patrol agents on the border and in the interior of the United States in some of the most challenging conditions the agency has ever faced.” Bovino went on to add, “Watching these agents out there giving it their all in some of the most dangerous of environments we have ever faced was humbling.”" target="_blank" >Breitbart</a> he plans to retire at the end of the month, and other outlets have since reported the news. The Sun-Times hasn’t independently verified those reports. A DHS spokesperson said, “Chief Bovino has not submitted any retirement paperwork.”</p><p>Bovino became <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/12/gregory-bovino-border-patrol-deportation-elcentro-california-blowing-rock-boone-north-carolina-migrants-immigration" target="_blank" >the face of the Trump administration’s controversial immigration enforcement efforts</a>, using social media to tout arrests and take on critics, including Pritzker. Agents under his command in Chicago made allegedly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/10/17/gregory-bovino-border-customs-enforcement-deportation-trump-california-chicago" target="_blank" >race-based stops</a>, used <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/14/ice-bovino-border-patrol-homeland-security-chicago-police-department" target="_blank" >risky tactics and pummeling force</a> and often deployed chemical irritants against protesters.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis ultimately <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >restricted the feds’ use of force</a> under Bovino’s watch in an order that was formally vacated earlier this month by a federal appeals court. Ellis notably accused Bovino about lying under oath about his justification for the use of tear gas in Little Village.</p><p>Bovino was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/26/border-patrol-gregory-bovino-tom-homan-immigration-alex-pretti" target="_blank" >sent back to the El Centro Sector</a> in Southern California following the killing of Alex Pretti on Jan. 24 in Minneapolis. Pretti, a nurse for the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, was fatally shot by two Customs and Border Protection agents.</p><p>After the shooting, Bovino said Pretti “approached law enforcement with a weapon” and sought to “massacre” them — a claim that was quickly undercut by video evidence, though Pretti was legally carrying a weapon.</p><p>Bovino was hired before July 6, 2008, making him <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbp.gov/employee-resources/retirement/leo-cbpo/cbpo-retirement" target="_blank" >exempt from the agency’s mandatory retirement</a> — which is the last day of the month in which a CBP employee both turns 57 and reaches 20 years of service. He turns 56 later this month.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/12/gregory-bovino-border-patrol-deportation-elcentro-california-blowing-rock-boone-north-carolina-migrants-immigration" target="_blank" >Greg Bovino’s the star of Trump’s deportation show. We trace his roots.</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="Judge blasts Trump’s Chicago border ‘Blitz,’ extends curbs on use of force that ‘shocks the conscience’" target="_blank" >Judge blasts Trump’s Chicago border ‘Blitz,’ extends curbs on use of force that ‘shocks the conscience’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/14/ice-bovino-border-patrol-homeland-security-chicago-police-department" target="_blank" >Tear gas, car crashes, chokeholds: Risky tactics have driven Trump’s Chicago deportation ‘blitz’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
author: Violet Miller

title: Remaining ‘Broadview Six’ defendants want conspiracy charge tossed, argue protesting isn’t a crime
summary: <p>Arguing that federal prosecutors have made a “crime out of what under the Constitution cannot be a crime,” the group of protesters<b> </b>originally known as the "Broadview Six" asked a judge Monday to toss the conspiracy charge<b> </b>filed against them because it runs afoul of the First Amendment’s freedom of assembly.</p><p>It’s the latest attempt to challenge the indictment brought against the group<b> </b>— and one that a defendant in the case had an active role in drafting. The prosecution is one of several to result from the Trump administration's Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign.</p><p>The group is now down to four, after prosecutors<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >dropped<b> </b>the charges against<b> </b>two</a> of the defendants last week. Those who remain say the government’s allegations of conspiracy — a felony that could lead to a prison sentence of up to six years — enhances a misdemeanor charge based on the defendants’ “exercise of their First Amendment rights of assembly and association.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" >Broadview 4? Feds drop conspiracy charges against 2 ICE protesters, including Dem who ended campaign</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-hangRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" </div><p>“That a misdemeanor … can be escalated to a felony conspiracy charge simply because it occurred in the midst of an otherwise peaceable assembly creates a substantial risk of chilling the public’s willingness to exercise their First Amendment rights of freedom of assembly and freedom of speech,” defense attorneys wrote in an 18-page motion<b> </b>filed Monday.</p><p>The motion was filed on behalf of all the remaining defendants. But one of them, Oak Park village trustee and lawyer Brian Straw, played an active role in drafting it. That's according to Straw attorney Christopher Parente, who said Straw invested "a lot of his blood, sweat and tears."</p><p>"I think the bigger issue for Brian is the right for people to peacefully assemble and to protest their government, regardless of what the issue is," Parente told the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>Charged along with Straw are 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt, congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh,<b> </b>and a senior member of Abughazaleh's campaign staff, Andre Martin. Abughazaleh is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/02/25/congressional-9th-district-15-democrats-march-17-primary-jan-schakowsky-seat" target="_blank" >seeking the Democratic nomination</a><b> </b>in Tuesday’s primary for Illinois’ 9th District<b> </b>congressional seat.</p><p>Prosecutors last week dropped charges against Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh, a musician, and Catherine “Cat” Sharp, a Democrat who dropped her bid for Cook County Board to focus on her legal defense. The feds also recently narrowed<b> </b>their theory of the case.</p><p>Challenges have followed in recent days from the four defendants who still face trial May 26. They sought records Friday<b> </b>that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >might show an improper influence</a> on the case<b> </b>by the Trump administration.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" >Remaining Broadview 6 defendants want records showing Trump administration’s influence on conspiracy case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Now they’ve asked U.S. District Judge April Perry<b> </b>to toss the conspiracy charge on First Amendment grounds, arguing that the feds' theory "puts any protester at risk of being charged with a felony on account of being in the wrong place at the wrong time with others." The lawyers are due back in Perry’s courtroom March 31. Each of the four also face a misdemeanor charge alleging they impeded an officer.</p><p>The conspiracy charge revolves around events on the morning of Sept. 26 outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility<b> </b>in Broadview. It became a hotbed for protests during Midway Blitz.</p><p>The indictment alleges that, while a federal agent drove a vehicle<b> </b>toward the ICE facility, the defendants and others surrounded it. Members of the larger crowd allegedly<b> </b>banged on the vehicle, pushed against it, scratched it and even etched the word “PIG”<b> </b>into it.</p><p>The crowd allegedly broke a side mirror<b> </b>and a rear windshield wiper<b> </b>and forced the agent “to drive at an extremely slow rate of speed.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> blitz</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But defense attorneys say none of the damage<b> </b>was caused by the defendants themselves — a point they expect prosecutors<b> </b>to concede. Rather, the indictment generally accuses the four of bracing themselves with their hands and bodies against the vehicle,<b> </b>hindering its progress.</p><p>They did so after exercising their First Amendment rights “in a location specified for such protests by the Village of Broadview,” and after the agent decided to slowly drive<b> </b>into the crowd, according to the defense attorneys.</p><p>The agent did not wait for police to clear a path, did not identify himself and did not order the crowd to move aside, the attorneys argued.</p><p>“Their only actions — aside from bracing themselves against a vehicle that drove into a crowd of protesters — was being in that crowd of protesters,” the defense attorneys wrote. “Their actions are inseparable from the exercise of their constitutional right to assemble — in the exact location where Broadview police had allowed them to do so all morning."</p><p>Evan<b> </b>Bernick, an associate professor<b> </b>at Northern Illinois University<b> </b>College of Law, said he spoke with Straw<b> </b>and his attorneys<b> </b>about the motion filed Monday. He said the allegations in the case could have a chilling effect on protests beyond those against Midway Blitz. That's because of the concern that lawful protesters could be on the hook for the illegal actions of others through a conspiracy charge.</p><p>"This prosecution is not just about this prosecution," Bernick said. "It's about the prosecution of anybody who might go into public and engage in an assembly with peaceful purposes, with lawful purposes, and then decide not to on the belief that they might get targeted and successfully indicted, even though they have done nothing wrong."</p>

title: Chicago and suburban Democratic voters more likely to vote for candidates who fought ICE, poll finds
summary: <p>Democratic and independent voters still see immigration enforcement as a top issue in Chicago and the surrounding suburbs — and are more likely to support a candidate who protested President Donald Trump’s "Operation Midway Blitz," a new poll commissioned by a progressive coalition found.</p><p>Several candidates in congressional and state races have made their anti-Immigration and Customs Enforcement stance a focal point of their campaigns, including the top U.S. Senate Democratic candidates. Tuesday’s primary elections will serve as a test of whether campaign messaging about fighting ICE worked — and how views on immigration have changed during Trump’s second term.</p><p>When voters were asked about ICE, 63% had an unfavorable view, while 31% had a favorable view. That broke down sharply by political parties, with 90% of Democrats viewing ICE unfavorably compared to 9% of Republicans. Among independents, the number was 62%. </p><p>In Chicago, 75% of those polled overall had an unfavorable view of ICE. In the rest of Cook County, 62% of those polled viewed ICE unfavorably, and in surrounding counties, 56% had an unfavorable view of ICE. </p><p>About 70% of likely Democratic primary voters who participated in the poll said a candidate’s position on ICE was the most important issue or very important to how they’d cast their vote. Nearly two-thirds of respondents said they’d be more likely to support a candidate who has been active in anti-ICE protests.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/voter-guide-primary-election-illinois/" >2026 Illinois Primary Elections Voter Guide</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>About 14% of participants said they resisted ICE actions themselves, and about a quarter of the others said they wished they could have done more. Those who took action were more likely to be younger Chicago residents who consider themselves liberal voters.</p><p>Those actions included signing anti-ICE petitions (32%), contacting local officials (27%), joining vigils or protests (24%), tracking ICE locally (16%) and blowing whistles to alert their neighbors to ICE presence (11%).</p><p>The survey of 800 registered voters in the Chicago media market, including Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Kane, Kankakee, Kendall, McHenry and Will counties, was taken March 1-4. Interviews were conducted by live phone calls and text-to-web responses. According to the pollster, self-described Democrats outnumbered Republicans in the sample 44% to 22%. Another 33% identifying as independent voters.</p><p>Of those polled, 33% approved of the job Trump is doing as president, while 64% disapproved. On Trump's handling of immigration, 35% approved, while 63% said they disapproved.</p><p>The poll was commissioned by Hands Off Chicago, a coalition of progressive community groups including the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, Equality Illinois and the Chicago Federation of Labor. The group also conducted four in-person focus groups — two with white progressives and liberals, one with Latinas and another with Black men. They also conducted an online focus group with swing voters.</p><p>Exposure to ICE played a role in voters’ reaction to the agency, with 73% of those who saw raids in their neighborhoods holding an unfavorable view of the agency. The number declined for those who didn’t have raids in their neighborhood, with 51% of those voters viewing ICE unfavorably.</p><p>The poll also found that 29% of Latinos said they saw ICE agents in their communities personally, more than twice the rate of Black or white voters.</p><p>About 75% of poll respondents said immigration is good for the country, with 83% saying they support providing a path to citizenship for people in the U.S. without documentation.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/01/31/brandon-johnson-investigate-ice-prosecution-executive-order-chicago" >Mayor Brandon Johnson orders CPD to investigate federal immigration agents for potential prosecution</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>At least 2,800 people were arrested in Illinois during "Operation Midway Blitz" between mid-September through mid-October, primarily in the Chicago area, according to ICE data obtained by the Data Deportation Project and statements about Border Patrol arrests made by the Justice Department in court. On Sept. 12, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/17/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-ice-dhs-trump-midway-blitz-shooting-homicide-franklin-park-chicago" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas González,</a> a father and cook originally from Mexico, was fatally shot at “close range” as he allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop. Operation Midway Blitz slowed in mid-November.</p>
author: Mitchell Armentrout

title: Broadview 4? Feds drop conspiracy charges against 2 ICE protesters, including Dem who ended campaign
summary: <p>Federal prosecutors on Thursday dropped conspiracy charges they’d filed against two<b> </b>of six people who protested outside a suburban<b> </b>immigration holding facility<b> </b>last fall,<b> </b>including a former Cook County Board candidate who dropped out of Tuesday's primary<b> </b>to fight the charges.</p><p>The group of defendants known as the “Broadview Six” will be down to four assuming U.S. District Judge April Perry grants the motion filed by federal prosecutors. It seeks to drop charges against <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/06/cook-county-board-candidate-suspends-campaign-to-fight-indictment" target="_blank" >Catherine “Cat” Sharp</a><b> </b>and musician Joselyn Walsh.</p><p>Sharp said the move "proves what we have always known — that the indictment in this case was flawed from the outset. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/12/kat-abughazaleh-operation-midway-blitz-donald-trump-jb-pritzker-brandon-johnson-other-candidates-face-arraignment-in-broadview-conspiracy-case" >‘We will win': Six Broadview protesters plead not guilty to conspiracy, decry attack on First Amendment</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>"While I am of course elated at this outcome, [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's] abuse of immigrants and refugees in our communities continues," she said.</p><p>Walsh said dismissal of the indictment "does not change the disruption it caused in my life for the past six months.</p><p>"It also does not change that I was a victim of ICE violence when they shot my guitar and that many continue to experience violence at the hands of federal agents," she said.</p><p>Assistant U.S. Attorney William Hogan wrote in Thursday's motion<b> </b>that, "as the United States attorney’s office does in every case, the government has continued to evaluate new facts, evidence, and information to ensure that the interests of justice are served.</p><p>“Accordingly, the United States hereby moves to dismiss with prejudice the indictment against Catherine Sharp and Joselyn Walsh, in the interests of justice,” he added.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" >Tracking every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s immigration blitz</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Still charged are<b> </b>congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh<b>, </b>Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw,<b> </b>45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt and Andre Martin. They are accused of a conspiracy to impede a federal officer.</p><p>Abughazaleh is seeking the Democratic nomination<b> </b>for Illinois’ 9th District congressional seat in Tuesday's primary.</p><p>The news comes after prosecutors said they planned to narrow and review the conspiracy case against the group. It means Sharp and Walsh <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >will join an ever-growing list</a> of people who have been cleared after being charged with nonimmigration crimes tied to Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>It is also a significant blow to the last remaining high-profile prosecution tied to the immigration enforcement campaign.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Arthur Maiorella/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago accused 32 known defendants of nonimmigration crimes connected to Midway Blitz. Once Perry grants the new motion pertaining to Sharp and Walsh,<b> </b>19 of the 32 will have been cleared. None of the 32 have been convicted, so far.</p><p>The cleared defendants include <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a>, the woman shot five times by a Border Patrol agent last October on the Southwest Side.<b> </b>Prosecutors dropped the case against her in November.</p><p>A jury also cleared <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/22/federal-jury-rejects-bovino-murder-plot-after-called-upon-stand-up-overreaching-government" target="_blank" >Juan Espinoza Martinez</a><b> </b>in January after he’d been accused of offering $10,000 for the murder of U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino. Immigration authorities took Espinoza Martinez<b> </b>into custody after his acquittal and have held him ever since.</p><p>But <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/27/chicago-ice-trump-bovino-marimar-martinez-crime-border-patrol-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >federal prosecution still comes at a cost</a>, even when charges are ultimately abandoned. In Sharp’s case, that includes the suspension of her campaign for Cook County Board so she could focus on her legal defense.</p><p>The remaining Broadview conspiracy defendants are set for trial<b> </b>May 26. The charges revolve around events on the morning of Sept. 26 outside the ICE facility in Broadview.</p><p>An indictment alleges that, while an agent drove a vehicle toward the facility, the defendants<b> </b>and others surrounded it. Members of the crowd allegedly banged on the vehicle, pushed against it, scratched it and even etched the word “PIG” into it.</p><p>The crowd allegedly broke a side mirror and a rear windshield wiper and forced the agent “to drive at an extremely slow rate of speed.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/27/chicago-ice-trump-bovino-marimar-martinez-crime-border-patrol-midway-blitz" >ICE protesters keep beating Trump in Chicago court, but the battles take a toll — ‘It’s about intimidation’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Prosecutors recently agreed to strike certain language from the indictment, though. They also acknowledged during a recent hearing that the timeframe of the alleged conspiracy is limited to Sept. 26, that it was “spontaneous” with no evidence of an explicit agreement, and that all potential co-conspirators were present in Broadview at the time.</p><p>Defense attorneys have said a key issue at trial could be the agent’s “decision and motivation to drive his vehicle into a crowd of more than 50 individuals who were peacefully protesting the documented atrocities occurring inside the Broadview facility.”</p><p>They’ve said their clients and others were engaged in a “Jericho Walk” supervised by local police, who helped traffic safely pass through the demonstration.</p><p>Eventually a Ford Expedition driven by an ICE agent turned “directly” into the crowd, according to the defense filings. There is no evidence the ICE agent waited for police assistance but opted instead to “drive directly into where the crowd was gathered,” defense attorneys say.</p>
author: Jon Seidel

title: Seeking special prosecutor to target ICE, coalition says O'Neill Burke turned 'blind eye' to feds' violence
summary: <p>Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen<b> </b>O’Neill<b> </b>Burke<b> </b>has turned a “blind eye”<b> </b>to “egregious acts of violence”<b> </b>by the federal agents behind last fall’s Operation Midway Blitz, a new coalition of more than 200 elected officials, clergy, journalists and attorneys argued in a court filing Thursday.</p><p>Despite demands that agents once led by U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/02/06/how-can-chicagos-top-prosecutor-hold-ice-accountable" target="_blank" >be prosecuted for state crimes</a> — like murder, assault, perjury<b> </b>or even conspiracy — O’Neill Burke has<b> </b>“never stated publicly that she has any intention to investigate these crimes,” they said.</p><p>That may be for fear of retaliation from President Donald Trump, they added.</p><p>That’s the argument made in a newly filed petition that makes the most aggressive pitch yet for a special prosecutor to investigate the agents who descended upon Chicago last fall. It was filed by the Loevy and Loevy<b> </b>law firm on behalf of a coalition that includes U.S. Reps. Jesus “Chuy” Garcia and Delia Ramirez, both Democrats, and former U.S. District Chief Judge Ruben Castillo, who was appointed to the bench in 1994 by President Bill Clinton.</p><p>It was filed Thursday in Cook County Circuit Court before<b> </b>Judge Erica<b> </b>Reddick, the presiding judge of the criminal division, ahead of a noon news conference.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/02/06/how-can-chicagos-top-prosecutor-hold-ice-accountable" >How can Chicago’s top prosecutor hold ICE accountable?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“Federal agents killed and maimed people, terrorized communities, and unleashed extreme force and chemical weapons indiscriminately against law-abiding residents who posed no threat to their safety,” the petition states,<b> </b>according to a copy obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>Meanwhile, “other state prosecutors in Illinois and around the country have initiated investigations into similar criminal conduct by federal agents … or announced their intention to investigate such conduct,” according to the petition.</p><p>It’s unclear whether a path to a special prosecutor exists for the coalition under the law. But O’Neill Burke says the petition will only make it more difficult for her office “to prosecute and win convictions” against agents who committed crimes during the deportation campaign.</p><p>“The stakes are too high for us to get this wrong,” O’Neill Burke, a Democrat, said in a statement earlier this week, “and I will strenuously oppose this petition.”</p><p>Still, it could increase the pressure on O’Neill Burke, even if unsuccessful. Loevy & Loevy used its lawsuit in federal court last fall to secure strategic wins, like court appearances and depositions from federal officials, as well as the public release of a tranche of records.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-600000" name="image-600000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Steve Art (left), attorney at Loevy & Loevy, alongside Craig Futterman, clinical professor of law at University of Chicago Law School, speaks in the lobby of the Dirksen Federal Courthouse on Jan. 8. Loevy & Loevy now represents a coalition seeking a special prosecutor to investigate and charge federal agents involved in Operation Midway Blitz.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>That’s even though the case was ultimately dismissed, and a federal appeals court vacated<b> </b>a sweeping preliminary injunction handed down by U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis.</p><p>Under the law, the new petition could lead to a hearing over whether O’Neill Burke has an actual conflict of interest. The petitioners also asked the judge for permission to “present a list of candidates” for special prosecutor or to “have input into the selection process.”</p><p>The coalition includes the Chicago News Guild, which represents journalists at the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>O’Neill Burke has publicly decried the actions of the Trump administration but maintains that her office is limited in its ability to prosecute on-duty federal agents.</p><p>She <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" >released her own guidance</a> for pursuing these sorts of cases last month after criticizing a plan put forth by Mayor Brandon Johnson, which her office argued raised major concerns of political interference.</p><p>Under her guidance, a law enforcement agency would lead a criminal investigation by collecting and preserving evidence. Then, prosecutors would conduct an independent review of all evidence and make charging decisions.</p><p>However, prosecuting federal agents<b> </b>in state court would require <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/08/can-state-officials-prosecute-the-feds-calls-grow-after-minneapolis-shooting" target="_blank" >showing<b> </b>that they acted unreasonably</a> while fulfilling their duties.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" >Cook County’s top prosecutor outlines plan to charge ICE agents with crimes</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>As of this week, O’Neill Burke’s office said no local agencies had brought cases against any on-duty immigration officials.</p><p>Prosecutors are entrusted with discretion to choose which cases they pursue. But the coalition argued O’Neill Burke’s impartiality “has been irrevocably tainted”<b> </b>by her failure to respond to public demands to investigate Midway Blitz agents.</p><p>“The residents of Cook County, citizens of Chicago, and elected officials at local, state, and federal levels have formalized public demands for the fair, impartial, and unencumbered investigation of allegations of criminal conduct by federal agents,” the petition states. “The state’s attorney has decided not to initiate any investigation.”</p><p>The group noted that O’Neill Burke works regularly with federal law enforcement. It also pointed to the Justice Department’s investigations of Trump’s political foes, including New York Attorney General Letitia James and Fani Willis, the district attorney in Fulton County, Georgia.</p><p>“At minimum, the threat of retaliation reduces public confidence that State’s Attorney [O’Neill Burke] will exercise her discretion fairly when determining whether to investigate or bring charges,” the coalition wrote in its petition.</p><p>“To expect her to investigate and prosecute federal agents who committed crimes in her own jurisdiction is highly improbable, as evidenced by her own inaction,” it added. “An independent special prosecutor, shielded from political conflict, is therefore necessary.”</p><p>The petition prominently recounts the Oct. 4 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >shooting of Marimar Martinez</a>, as well as the Sept. 12 killing<b> </b>of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/15/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-fatally-shot-by-ice-agents-touched-the-lives-of-so-many-loved-ones-say" target="_blank" >Silverio<b> </b>Villegas<b> </b>González</a>. In both instances, the coalition argued that agents “lied” about what happened.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5b80f98/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3110x1745+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb0%2F04%2F1db7d61747f79df87515c45fc1a5%2Fmartinez-260202-005.jpg"
