class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Marimar Martinez stands in the Chicago Public Media lobby at Navy Pier on Feb. 1. Martinez survived five gunshots from a Border Patrol agent in Chicago last fall. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Christopher<b> </b>Parente, Martinez’s attorney, recently said there is an ongoing investigation<b> </b>into Border Patrol agent Charles Exum, who shot Martinez five times on the Southwest Side. The investigation is being handled by<b> </b>the U.S. attorney’s office<b> </b>in South Bend, Indiana, Parente said.</p><p>It’s unclear where that investigation stands, though. Parente told the Sun-Times, "we remain hopeful that the federal government will do its job and conduct a full and fair investigation of Marimar's shooting."</p><p>"If the federal government fails to carry out its mission as promised in Marimar's case, Cook County must be empowered to pick up the mantle of leadership and ensure justice is done for Marimar and all other victims of federal agent misconduct," Parente said.</p><p>The coalition’s petition catalogs alleged batteries, assaults, kidnappings and other violence at the hands of federal agents. It even makes a case for conspiracy charges, alleging that agents “undertook coordinated efforts over the course of hours, days, and months to commit serious crimes against the citizens and residents of Cook County.”</p><p>Though court precedent shows that a “political alliance” can create a conflict of interest, it also notes that a petitioner must plead “specific facts”<b> </b>to show a state’s attorney “would not zealously represent” the people.</p><p>A petitioner could also show<b> </b>that a state’s attorney has abandoned her duty through “an impropriety or insufficiency in the state’s attorney’s investigation,” according to past rulings.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/08/can-state-officials-prosecute-the-feds-calls-grow-after-minneapolis-shooting" >Can state officials prosecute the feds? Calls grow after Minneapolis shooting</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Special prosecutors have been used in the past in response to potential conflicts of interest or alleged misconduct within the Cook County state’s attorney’s office. Often they’re appointed to investigate and prosecute specific cases. </p><p>In 2016, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/crime/2016/06/02/judge-to-appoint-special-prosecutor-in-laquan-mcdonald-case" target="_blank" ><u>a special prosecutor took over the murder case against Chicago Police Officer Jason Van Dyke</u></a>, who fatally shot 17-year-old Laquan McDonald. Civil rights lawyers had long questioned former Cook County State’s Attorney Anita Alvarez’s objectivity in the case and criticized her for taking more than a year to charge Van Dyke. But a special prosecutor was only appointed after Alvarez lost re-election and recused herself from the case. </p><p>In 2019, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/8/23/20828849/jussie-smollett-special-prosecutor-dan-webb" target="_blank" ><u>a special prosecutor was assigned to reopen the Jussie Smollett case</u></a> and investigate former Cook County State’s Attorney Kim Foxx’s handling of the charges. The special prosecutor secured a conviction against Smollett for lying about an alleged hate crime, but it was overturned years later.</p><p>There have also been examples of special prosecutors given much broader assignments, though. In 2002, a special prosecutor was appointed to investigate decades of allegations against former Chicago Police Cmdr. Jon Burge. The special prosecutor found that Burge and his crew had tortured nearly 200 people during the 1970s to the 1990s. But the statute of limitations had run out on many of the crimes, making them unable to prosecute.</p><p><i>Neither the reporters nor editors who worked on this story — including some represented by the News Guild — have been involved in the litigation described in this article.</i></p>
author: Sophie Sherry

title: CPS should work to prevent future attendance drops due to immigration enforcement, community groups say
summary: <p>A coalition of community groups and a parent advocacy organization are urging Chicago Public Schools to take steps now to prevent attendance declines should there be another surge in federal immigration enforcement.</p><p>Among the things they are asking for: More frequent updates about attendance trends and designated safe spaces where students and parents can retreat should they encounter a threat while going to or from school.</p><p>“So much was needed for our families that we were not prepared for,” said Ana Lorenzana of the Northwest Center in Belmont Cragin, who spoke Wednesday during a virtual briefing on <a class="Link" href="https://kidsfirstchicago.org/assets/miscellaneous/2026-K1C-Safe-Passage-report-v5.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>a report that her organization and several others worked to produce</u></a>.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/10/chicago-immigration-deport-trump-noem-bovino-midway-blitz" target="_blank" ><u>It is unclear whether President Donald Trump</u></a> will ramp up the number of agents in Chicago and employ the kind of aggressive tactics that ravaged immigrant communities with fear this past fall. For now, there are no signs of a spring surge, as these tactics are under scrutiny and top officials, including U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino, are no longer in their positions.</p><p>But if it does happen, the school system needs to be ready, unlike in the fall when the response was, according to the report, “uneven, fragile, and unsustainable.”</p><p>“The good news is that we have time to prepare,”said Daniel Anello, chief executive director of the parent advocacy organization Kids First Chicago, which spearheaded the report. “I think the bad news is we don't have too much time to prepare, given where we are, and we really need to get organized.”</p><p>Kids First Chicago partnered with the <a class="Link" href="https://authenticengagement.info/" target="_blank" ><u>Coalition for Authentic Community Engagement</u></a>, a group that includes the pastors of prominent Black churches and organizations that serve or represent many of the city’s immigrant communities, including Chinese Americans and Middle Eastern refugees.</p><p>CPS officials said they appreciate the report’s focus on collaboration and will evaluate its recommendations.</p><p>“We remain committed to working alongside all partners to strengthen our practices and ensure educators and students can thrive in a secure environment,” a CPS spokesperson wrote in a statement.</p><p>While CPS has regularly stated that overall attendance did not suffer much this fall, the report’s authors reached a conclusion similar to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/12/02/as-immigration-agents-swept-chicago-this-fall-communities-stepped-in-to-get-kids-to-school-safely" target="_blank" ><u>a WBEZ and Sun-Times analysis earlier this school year</u></a>: There were spikes in absenteeism on particular days and weeks.</p><p>Higher-than-usual absenteeism among English Language Learners was a particular problem, the group found. In the seventh week of school, 3,000 more English Language Learners stayed home, compared to previous years, they estimated.</p><p>Marlon Henriquez, principal of Gunsaulus Scholastic Academy, a magnet school in the Southwest Side neighborhood of Brighton Park, said once the federal enforcement activity died down, attendance bounced back at the elementary school.</p><p>“Our families want to come to school,” he said. “That is very clear.”</p><p>But attendance among high school students who are English Language Learners has not fully rebounded, Anello said. He said “there’s more work to be done” to re-engage those students.</p><p>The report lays out several recommendations, including prioritizing getting support to communities where there has been a lot of immigration enforcement and, consequently, high absenteeism.</p><p>In these communities especially, the report calls for CPS to publish weekly attendance reports so issues are spotted more quickly.</p><p>The report’s authors say principals and other top staff should get <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2025/09/05/volunteers-on-ice-patrol-in-chicagos-pilsen-neighborhood-looking-for-agents" target="_blank" ><u>rapid response training</u></a> and schools should have an arrival and dismissal team with a designated leader who can make sure a protocol is followed when there are threats of federal agents nearby.</p><p>Kids First and the community groups also want CPS to do more to get students to school. They point out that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/12/02/as-immigration-agents-swept-chicago-this-fall-communities-stepped-in-to-get-kids-to-school-safely" target="_blank" ><u>communities stepped up this fall</u></a>, providing walking school buses, carpools and neighborhood watches. But they say the district needs a more coordinated approach.</p><p>Henriquez said where he lives on the North Side, a lot of residents came out to keep watch over children as they went to and from school. But Gunsaulus is in an area filled with immigrants and residents who were too scared to stand outside and be those eyes and ears.</p><p>“Getting to school and leaving school, that's something that's out of our sphere of control,” he said. “Having individuals present, opening doors, saying good morning, saying goodbye, being a familiar happy face, would make a huge impact in the community of Gunsaulus.”</p><p>The groups say CPS should undo <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/08/13/cps-safe-passage" target="_blank" ><u>recent cuts to the Safe Passage program</u></a>, which posts people on corners to watch students go to and from school, and pilot a transportation program that could be used during surges. That could include working with trusted community organizations to shuttle students to school or expanding bus routes, the report says.</p><p>The groups also suggest that school safety committees made up of teachers and other staff be paired with groups of parents who want to be involved.</p><p>Finally, they want CPS to step up its support for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/12/no-recess-lockdowns-less-learning-how-immigration-agents-disrupted-cps-schools-this-fall" target="_blank" ><u>students impacted by federal immigration activity</u></a>. They say CPS should expand mental health services and refer students for food and economic support “so temporary fear does not create long-term academic harm.”</p><p>They also say CPS should make sure students have laptops and a reliable internet connection to allow for some remote learning or tutoring if individual students are facing a real safety risk to come to school in person.</p>
author: Sarah Karp | WBEZ

title: Feds dispute Skokie woman's claim she was held by ICE for 30 hours
summary: <p>The Department of Homeland Security is disputing the story of Sundas “Sunny” Naqvi, a U.S. citizen from Skokie who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/08/skokie-woman-citizen-sunny-naqvi-detained-customs-border-patrol-ohare-immigration-ice" target="_blank" ><u>claimed she and her colleagues were detained</u></a> for more than 30 hours by federal immigration authorities over the weekend.</p><p>The federal agency claimed she was released nearly an hour after she was flagged for secondary screening at O'Hare Airport Thursday. The agency posted photos on social media Wednesday evening purporting to prove that. But Kevin Morrison, a Cook County commissioner and Naqvi's friend since high school, told the Chicago Sun-Times the photos were doctored.</p><p>"Instead of releasing a clearly doctored photo, I call on DHS to release all of the relevant video at O’Hare Airport at the days and times in question," Morrison said in a statement Wednesday evening.</p><p>On Sunday, Morrison shared Naqvi's version of events at a news conference outside the ICE processing facility in suburban Broadview. He said Naqvi and five of her colleagues were detained at O’Hare by federal immigration agents for their “recent travel history” after returning from Istanbul.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <blockquote class="bluesky-embed" data-bluesky-uri="at://did:plc:ddphbgeot3wsgicyuvx3q67n/app.bsky.feed.post/3mgh3v4u7m22n" data-bluesky-cid="bafyreigrh2habaoourg5hrsbdcqbhkqhm6qqygyhgnb24tsiucu2ardpqe"><p lang="en">UPDATE: An attorney I am in contact with, asked for her cell phone number to share with someone with the US Attorney General‘s office to try to find the phone in the facility, conveniently enough shortly after her phone unlocks she sends out this text message 1/3</p>— <a href="https://bsky.app/profile/did:plc:ddphbgeot3wsgicyuvx3q67n?ref_src=embed">Kevin Morrison (@morrisonforil.bsky.social)</a> <a href="https://bsky.app/profile/did:plc:ddphbgeot3wsgicyuvx3q67n/post/3mgh3v4u7m22n?ref_src=embed">2026-03-07T05:30:03.234Z</a></blockquote><script async src="https://embed.bsky.app/static/embed.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div></div><p>Naqvi, 28, and the others were taken to the Broadview facility where they were then transferred to a facility in Dodge County, Wisconsin, sometime Friday evening, Morrison said. She was released around 5 a.m. Saturday after nearly 30 hours.</p><p>The Cook County Sheriff’s office said it searched the facility and found nothing. The Dodge County, Wisconsin, sheriff's office didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Naqvi and her detained colleagues declined interviews with the Sun-Times at the news conference Sunday and declined to comment by phone Wednesday. Naqvi’s lawyer, Rob Held, also did not return calls.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/30/new-body-camera-footage-shows-aftermath-of-ice-officer-allegedly-attacking-activist-near-chicago" target="_blank" ><u></u></a><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/28/broadview-police-say-theyre-investigating-feds-over-attack-on-cbs-reporters-vehicle" target="_blank" ><u></u></a><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/11/13/lawyer-seeking-preliminary-injunction-in-lawsuit-against-broadview-over-protest-hours-appears-outside-ice-facility" target="_blank" ><u></u></a><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/30/new-body-camera-footage-shows-aftermath-of-ice-officer-allegedly-attacking-activist-near-chicago" target="_blank" ><u></u></a></p><p>The Department of Homeland Security first dismissed Naqvi's claims in a statement Monday, calling the story “blatantly false." The agency said she arrived at O’Hare Thursday at 10:21 a.m., was referred to secondary screening for three minutes, retrieved her bags and departed the airport at 11:43 a.m. The agency said the entire exchange was captured on video.</p><p>The agency said it contacted her on Friday to ask her to inform people she was OK and confirmed that the Cook County Sheriff’s office had contacted the Broadview ICE processing facility about her.</p><p>The federal agency also pointed to Naqvi's criminal record. Naqvi pleaded guilty in 2022 to making a false police report alleging sexual assault and served two years probation, according to count records. The case was then dismissed as part of a deferred prosecution agreement.</p><p>On Tuesday, the agency said, “Ms. Naqvi was not taken into custody or transferred to ICE for detention."</p><p>Late Wednesday, the Department of Homeland Security <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/DHSgov/status/2031879248068194404?s=20" target="_blank" ><u>posted screenshots</u></a> on social media purporting to show Naqvi exiting secondary screening.</p><p>Morrison said they contained a "clearly doctored photo" and called on the agency to release all of its video.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">HERE ARE THE RECEIPTS:<br><br>As we said Sunny Naqvi entered the CBP area at 10:21 am.<br><br>Surveillance footage from O’Hare CLEARLY shows her entering secondary inspection at 10:46 a.m., and leaving secondary to the public area at 11:42 a.m.<br><br>Her claims of spending 43 hours in DHS custody… <a href="https://t.co/GkqWBLS6sn">https://t.co/GkqWBLS6sn</a> <a href="https://t.co/SWOJmMulcy">pic.twitter.com/SWOJmMulcy</a></p>— Homeland Security (@DHSgov) <a href="https://twitter.com/DHSgov/status/2031879248068194404?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">March 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Morrison isn't alone in questioning the federal agency’s credibility.</p><p>A federal judge found that former U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" ><u>lied in a court deposition</u></a> in November about his own use of tear gas in a confrontation with protesters in Little Village. And 17 of 32 defendants in federal cases related to Operation Midway Blitz <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" ><u>have been dismissed</u></a>, three of which came after grand juries <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/10/federal-grand-jury-rejects-another-midway-blitz-case-this-time-against-laugh-factory-manager?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=12112025%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=12112025%20Morning%20Edition+CID_249b96e5ffb43cc073e9614d6b1b88f8&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Case%20rejected&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" ><u>refused to indict</u></a>.</p><p>Shortly after agents shot Silverio Villegas González to death last September in Franklin Park, DHS claimed an agent was “seriously injured” after allegedly being dragged by González's vehicle. But police body-camera video later showed the agent said he was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/09/22/ice-officer-injuries-nothing-major-deadly-franklin-park-shooting-mexican-immigrant-chicago-video" target="_blank" ><u>“just shooken up a little</u></a>.”</p><p>Footage released in February also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/10/marimar-martinez-the-chicago-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-expected-to-file-lawsuit-release-evidence" target="_blank" ><u>contradicted the agency’s account</u></a> of when one of its agents shot Marimar Martinez in Brighton Park last fall. DHS later said it “stands by our press releases and statements. The facts of what happened did not change.”</p>
author: Mohammad Samra

Gregory Bovino left town last fall, Chicago’s reprieve came with a warning: The tear gas, chaos and fear associated with Operation Midway Blitz could return fourfold this month. Now March is here, and President Donald Trump has fired U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, while Bovino was put on the sidelines in January after federal officers' fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis.</p><p><b>After the blitz</b>: A source told the Chicago Sun-Times in November that 1,000 agents could return this month. title: Another Trump administration deportation blitz hasn’t materialized in Chicago
summary: <p>When U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino<b> </b>left town last fall, Chicago’s reprieve came with a warning: The tear gas, chaos and fear associated with Operation Midway Blitz could return to the city’s streets<b> </b>fourfold<b> </b>in March.</p><p>Now March is here. And President Donald Trump has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/05/trump-fires-noem-dhs-ice-border-patrol-markwayne-mullin" target="_blank" >fired Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem</a>, instead.</p><p>Bovino’s out too. The White House put him on the sidelines in January after the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal officers<b> </b>in Minneapolis. Even Tricia<b> </b>McLaughlin<b>, </b>the assistant secretary who once fiercely defended Homeland Security, has moved on.</p><p>All told, there’s little on the horizon to suggest Operation Midway Blitz 2.0 is about to materialize.</p><p>Much has changed since a source told the Chicago Sun-Times<b> </b>in November<b> </b>that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2025/11/11/u-s-border-patrol-boss-greg-bovino-fellow-agents-expected-to-soon-leave-chicago" target="_blank" >1,000 agents could return</a><b> </b>this month.<b> </b>The enforcement surge in Minnesota that followed the earlier Chicago campaign<b> </b>turned out to be a breaking point, leaving the Trump administration struggling to justify the shooting deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.</p><p>Calls to reform immigration enforcement<b> </b>have led to a partial government shutdown. Senate Democrats last week blocked<b> </b>Homeland Security funding<b> </b>for a third time,<b> </b>refusing to approve a spending bill without<b> </b>stricter use-of-force policies and a ban on officers wearing masks.</p><p>Steve Art, an attorney<b> </b>who challenged the feds’ tactics<b> </b>in court last fall, said the Minneapolis campaign gave the American people<b> </b>"a look at what we saw in Chicago throughout Operation Midway Blitz."</p><p>And, he said,<b> </b>"the American people didn’t like it."</p><p>The Chicago operation featured roving bands of masked agents, thousands of arrests, the seemingly indiscriminate use of tear gas and pepper balls, and two shootings, one of which claimed the life of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/12/ice-officer-fatally-shoots-man-during-traffic-stop-in-chicago-suburb-authorities-say" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas González</a>. </p><p>"Bovino being gone and Noem being gone within six months of the start of Operation Midway Blitz really shows you how politically untenable it is to engage in that kind of operation in the United States," Art said. "And that should give everybody a lot of hope."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-ac0000" name="html-embed-module-ac0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/27969115"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27969115/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>A Homeland Security spokesperson said officials in the department "do not discuss future or potential operations."</p><p>"Every day, DHS enforces the laws of the nation across the country including in Chicago," the spokesperson added.</p><p>Immigration enforcement remains a key pillar of Trump’s second term. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has a mountain of funding and continues to hire and increase its capacity<b> </b>to remove immigrants from the country, according to a former Homeland Security official.</p><p>The feds are still fighting a court order that would govern the treatment of people held<b> </b>in an immigration processing facility<b> </b>in Broadview. Last fall, a judge heard<b> </b>that<b> </b>people were crammed<b> </b>100 at a time<b> </b>into a cell there, with nowhere to sleep<b> </b>but a dirty floor<b> </b>near an open toilet.</p><p>Art said it’s good to be prepared for another surge in enforcement. But he also warned of future issues "relating to the election and to polling places." </p><p>Meanwhile, in the nation’s capital, U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez<b> </b>said Democrats<b> </b>"can’t keep sabotaging ourselves." She took Noem to task<b> </b>in a fiery meeting<b> </b>last month<b> </b>and told her, "your days may be numbered."</p><p>That was eight days before<b> </b>Trump showed Noem the door.</p><p>Now, with Homeland Security on its heels, Ramirez told the Sun-Times "this is our moment."</p><p>"Our strategy has to be, delay as far as you possibly can," the Illinois Democrat said. "Delay till November, if you can. Maybe January. And then let us get into the majority."</p><h3><b>Changing tactics</b></h3><p>The public outcry<b> </b>that stifled the feds’ immigration operation<b> </b>in Minneapolis<b> </b>led to<b> </b>new<b> </b>ICE directives<b> </b>that were relayed during<b> </b>recent<b> </b>agency-wide leadership meetings, the former Homeland Security official<b> </b>told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Leaders were told to prioritize<b> </b>"targeted enforcement,"<b> </b>instead of the "street sweeps" and large-scale campaigns like Midway Blitz, the official said. That would mean a return to ICE’s traditional, but still aggressive, enforcement tactics.</p><p>It would also mean setting aside the hallmark, but controversial, tactics of Midway Blitz: Roaming Chicago’s neighborhoods and stopping anyone whose legal status appeared to be in doubt. Those tactics came roaring back Dec. 16, when Bovino led Border Patrol agents on a brief trip to the Chicago area.</p><p>ICE still has vast financial resources and access to vital information from other government agencies that helps agents identify and target people.</p><p>“Does the Chicago field office just really try to do a lot of enforcement without supplemental folks from other areas and other federal agencies?” the former official said. “Do they look at different ways of arresting people, like worksites?”</p><p>“It doesn’t appear that they’re going to stop doing immigration enforcement because they’re ramping up all the other parts of the system.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>There’s no obvious sign of another Chicago surge within Homeland Security spending, though. Last summer,<b> </b>the agency stocked up on office supplies and ammunition to be used<b> </b>here, while also investing in relocation services for agents, according to federal data.</p><p>Similar purchases were made in Minnesota and North Carolina in the months leading up to increased immigration enforcement<b> </b>in those states.</p><p>The department has continued buying supplies and security equipment in Minnesota over the past month, as large swaths of agents remain in the area.</p><p>But the department<b> </b>hasn’t made any major purchases<b> </b>for use<b> </b>here<b> </b>since the withdrawal<b> </b>of Bovino and many of his agents<b> </b>in November.</p><p>The last contract<b> </b>the department signed<b> </b>related to the Broadview holding facility<b> </b>was a $349,000<b> </b>purchase<b> </b>for box lunch services<b> </b>on Dec. 8.</p><p>Those services are set to expire in early April.</p><h3><b>Plans for polling places?</b></h3><p>The spending impasse in Washington leaves immigration enforcement largely unaffected. That’s because the agencies at the crux of the argument are considered essential under a shutdown.</p><p>That includes ICE, which received<b> </b>$75 billion<b> </b>in Trump’s major tax and spending bill, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That also allows the agency to ride out the funding lapse while other departments under Homeland Security will be forced to furlough workers and cut operations.</p><p>Chicago Democrats<b> </b>like Ramirez<b> </b>hope the impasse — and Noem’s firing — will delay any plans to target Chicago in another sweeping immigration operation. Trump said he would nominate U.S. Sen. Markwayne<b> </b>Mullin, R-Oklahoma, as his next Homeland Security secretary.</p><p>But Ramirez said Mullin<b> </b>is unlikely to be confirmed by the Senate until some time in April.</p><p>“Frankly, it wouldn't work well with them if they end up continuing these big operations without a leader at the helm,” Ramirez said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Delia Ramirez speaks during a World Refugee Day ceremony at Daley Plaza on June 18, 2025.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Lawmakers in the nation’s capital have also raised concerns about the Trump administration using ICE or Border Patrol agents to disrupt voting in November. U.S. Sen. Chris<b> </b>Coons<b> </b>asked Noem last week, before she was fired, whether she would rule out<b> </b>deploying agents<b> </b>to polling places.</p><p>“There are no plans to have ICE officers at our polling locations,” Noem told the Delaware<b> </b>Democrat.</p><p>Coons cited a law<b> </b>forbidding troops at the polls<b> </b>and continued to press Noem on whether she would “rule it out.”<b> </b>Noem retorted, “do you plan on illegal aliens voting in our elections, senator?”</p><p>Others share Coons’ concern. Art said plans are in the works<b> </b>to litigate<b> </b>“whether there’s ever a reason to have federal forces, like we saw during Operation Midway Blitz, anywhere near a polling place.”</p><p>“We think the obvious answer to that, under the law, is no,” Art said.<b> </b>“But it’s our intention to litigate that issue far in advance.”</p><p>Art helped win<b> </b>last fall’s<b> </b>order<b> </b>from U.S. District Judge<b> </b>Sara Ellis<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >restricting<b> </b>the feds’ use of force</a> during<b> </b>Midway Blitz — an order <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/b3/26/ced883424be7b53aa5b8d9586922/chc7thorderuse.pdf" target="_blank" >formally vacated<b> </b>last week</a> by the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. Art's team also secured<b> </b>an under-oath deposition<b> </b>from Bovino, during which Ellis said<b> </b>he lied<b> </b>about his justification<b> </b>for the use of tear gas<b> </b>in Little Village.</p><h3><b>‘They say they’re coming back’</b></h3><p>The ICE holding facility in Broadview became a focal point of Midway Blitz. Not only did many of the feds’ detainees find themselves held there at some point, but it became the site of near-daily protests.</p><p>Designed as a short-term holding facility, U.S. District Judge Robert<b> </b>Gettleman<b> </b>remarked last November that it had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/04/claims-of-unsanitary-black-hole-conditions-at-broadviews-ice-facility-to-be-heard-by-federal-judge" target="_blank" >“really become a prison.”</a><b> </b>He did so while presiding over a lawsuit that alleges the feds were “warehousing people at Broadview for days on end.”</p><p>Gettleman handed down a temporary restraining order<b> </b>that month<b> </b>aimed at improving conditions inside the facility.<b> </b>He required<b> </b>a clean mat<b> </b>and bedding<b> </b>for everyone<b> </b>held there overnight,<b> </b>and that cells<b> </b>be cleaned<b> </b>twice daily.</p><p>The order is still in effect. A two-day<b> </b>hearing<b> </b>over whether Gettleman should enter a more permanent order<b> </b>is set to begin April 21.</p><p>But in mid-December, a month after Bovino and his agents first left town, the Justice Department seemed to have an opportunity to bring the case to an end. title: Chicago law firm leading push to appoint special prosecutor to target ICE, Border Patrol agents
summary: <p>A high-powered Chicago law firm that fought Operation Midway Blitz in federal court announced a plan Monday to push for the appointment of a special prosecutor to investigate and potentially charge the law enforcement officials who carried out the aggressive deportation campaign in the Chicago area.</p><p>The firm, Loevy and Loevy, said 200 individuals and organizations are supporting a petition to install an outsider in the office of Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke, who has spent weeks saying her staff can only go so far to target the feds.</p><p>The coalition plans to hold a news conference Thursday afternoon at Federal Plaza downtown, Loevy and Loevy said in a statement.</p><p>O’Neill Burke rebuked the call for a special prosecutor, slamming any petition as “frivolous [and] contrary to centuries of legal precedent and court rulings.”</p><p>“The reported plan to petition for a special prosecutor will make it more difficult for the Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office to prosecute and win convictions against [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] agents who break the law and secure justice for victims harmed by their conduct,” O’Neill Burke wrote in a statement.</p><p>“The stakes are too high for us to get this wrong, and I will strenuously oppose this petition.”</p><p>In its statement, Loevy and Loevy highlighted the extreme force used by federal immigration officials during the monthslong deportation campaign, referring to the on-duty actions as “crimes.” They cited widespread tear-gassing, attacks against “peaceful civilians” and shootings that wounded <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/11/evidence-shows-feds-lied-about-marimar-martinezs-shooting-in-chicago-attorney-says" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a> and killed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/17/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-ice-dhs-trump-midway-blitz-shooting-homicide-franklin-park-chicago" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas González</a>.</p><p>“Yet there has been no federal or state investigation or prosecution of any [of] the individuals who perpetrated these offenses,” the firm said. “An independent, special prosecutor is essential to ensure that there is accountability in Cook County.”</p><p>The demands for O'Neill Burke’s office to target federal agents are nothing new. In fact, another lawyer already filed a lawsuit earlier this year seeking to install a special prosecutor to handle such cases in county court. </p><p>O'Neill Burke has maintained that her office is limited in its ability to prosecute and secure convictions against on-duty federal agents. Still, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" >she released guidance</a> last month showing how she could pursue charges if a case were brought to her office. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> which includes elected officials, community organizations, journalists and other attorneys.</p><p>Loevy and Loevy was involved in a case last year in which U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis took the extraordinary step of issuing a preliminary injunction to rein in the feds’ aggressive actions. The injunction was <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/b3/26/ced883424be7b53aa5b8d9586922/chc7thorderuse.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>formally vacated</u><b><u> </u></b><u>last week</u></a> by the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.</p><p>Loevy and Loevy noted that sworn statements were submitted and hundreds of hours of video footage was compiled as part of federal court proceedings tied to Midway Blitz, indicating there’s already a pile of evidence waiting for a possible special prosecutor.</p><p>O’Neill Burke previously criticized Mayor Brandon Johnson's executive order directing the Chicago Police Department to go after federal agents, calling it "wholly inappropriate" because it instructed officers to make referrals to prosecutors "at the direction of the mayor's office." O'Neill Burke later released her own guidance last month. </p><p>Under the guidance, law enforcement agencies would lead criminal investigations by collecting and preserving evidence. Then, prosecutors would conduct an independent review of all evidence and make charging decisions, as they do in all felony cases. Her office said local law enforcement agencies haven't sought charges against any on-duty immigration officials.</p><p>O’Neill Burke noted on Monday that cases against the feds would be difficult to pursue, citing protections offered to on-duty agents and “challenges in acquiring evidence from federal law enforcement under this current administration.”</p><p>"My office’s goal is not to merely charge, but to successfully prosecute and convict criminal ICE agents,” O’Neill Burke said. “We are obligated to follow the law, evaluate evidence that is presented to us, and make a charging decision based on the facts.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/02/06/how-can-chicagos-top-prosecutor-hold-ice-accountable" target="_blank" >Veteran attorneys have been skeptical</a> about a judge’s ability to install a special prosecutor to investigate federal agents. Traditionally, special prosecutors are put in place when there is a conflict of interest or allegation of misconduct within the state’s attorney’s office.</p><p>The earlier petition for a special prosecutor, filed by attorney Sheryl Weikal, remains pending.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" >Cook County’s top prosecutor outlines plan to charge ICE agents with crimes</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/02/06/how-can-chicagos-top-prosecutor-hold-ice-accountable" target="_blank" >How can Chicago’s top prosecutor hold ICE accountable?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/06/eileen-oneill-burke-brandon-johnson-immigration-ice-law" target="_blank" >County’s top prosecutor calls Mayor Brandon Johnson’s ICE executive order ‘wholly inappropriate’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjuiidy-tlkjhhnv-q/" target="_blank" >Frank Main</a></h5><p><b>A way out</b>: Decades of undiagnosed mental illness beginning when Lottie Elliott was 15 led her to homelessness, her children being taken away and repeated arrests. In 2022, Elliott was offered a way to stop that damaging cycle through Bridges of Colorado, which places mental health liaisons in courtrooms across the state to help defendants whose persistent mental illness has contributed to repeated arrests.</p><p><b>Results</b>: Elliott says people from the Bridges program worked with her in jail until she was found to be competent to face criminal charges. The liaisons helped get her into a residential sober-living program with intensive therapy under the monitoring of a judge, who granted her probation. She’s now in her own apartment, has reunited with her son, is taking regular mental health medication and is helping others as a peer counselor.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: An Illinois task force of legislators, law enforcement, judiciary officials and mental health professionals is looking at Bridges of Colorado as a potential model for Illinois. They've been working to figure out how to improve the handling of criminal defendants with severe, persistent mental illness.</p><p><b>Chance to thrive</b>: "My life is incredibly humbling," Elliott says. "I want to share with people who were like me, who believed there was no hope and it was not possible. It is. We can recover."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/06/mentally-ill-downtown-killings-chicago-police-department-mental-health-care-bridges-colorado" title: U.S. citizen from Skokie stopped at O'Hare, detained by immigration officials for nearly 30 hours
summary: <p>A U.S. citizen from Skokie spent nearly 30 hours in custody by federal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration" >immigration</a> officials after she was detained at O'Hare Airport following a work trip Thursday, drawing rebukes from family, friends and politicians. </p><p>Sundas "Sunny" Naqvi and five colleagues, including two other U.S. citizens and three individuals with green cards, were all detained at the airport by federal immigration agents for their "recent travel history" after returning from Istanbul, Cook County commissioner and family friend Kevin Morrison told reporters outside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement center in Broadview Sunday. </p><p>Naqvi, 28, and the others were taken to the Broadview facility where they were then transferred to a facility in Dodge County, Wisconsin, sometime Friday evening, according to Morrison. She was then released around 5 a.m. Saturday after nearly 30 hours and a woman gave her a ride to a hotel where she reunited with family who followed her phone's location until service died. </p><p>"All she was told was that there was some curious travel history, but they had no cause to detain her for those 30 hours," Morrison said, adding that federal agents "lied to" local law enforcement and elected officials by saying Naqvi was never detained. </p><p>Immigration officials didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>"We need transparency, we need accountability and we need to make sure that we are incredibly mindful of the steps we must take as a nation to protect all of our civil rights and civil liberties," said Morrison. "The fact that this could happen to any U.S. citizen should terrify us all." </p><p>Naqvi's sister, Sarah Afzal, said she almost filed a missing persons report when she couldn’t get answers from local or federal police. </p><p>"She was right here and then she was in Wisconsin," Afzal said. "It was terrifying." </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/08/deportation-francisco-gonzalez-jasso-panchito-gang-latin-kings-deported-ice-mexico-midway-blitz-little-village" >Labeled a gang member and deported, longtime Chicagoan tries to restart in his Mexican hometown</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>A number of candidates running for Congress were on hand at Broadview to talk to news media, including 7th District candidate Reed Showalter and 9th District candidates Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss, Kat Abughazaleh, Bushra Amiwala and Illinois state Sen. Laura Fine.</p><p>"They were only brought home after their families and our community refused to back down and kept asking for answers," Abughazaleh said. "This is going to be the new normal if we don't stand up against it." </p><p>Fine called the arrests "completely unconscionable" and emphasized the importance of continued congressional oversight. </p><p>"We are not getting the full story, we are not getting all of the facts and it is up to Congress to dig deep into what's going on so we understand as citizens and as residents what is happening and [so] that we could get down to the truth," Fine said. </p><p>Amiwala, who knows Naqvi, praised the efforts by family and friends to seek the woman's release.</p><p>"For her to have a community that she does — that was able to rally this many people on such short span — is a testament and reflection to her and her family," Amiwala said. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/27/chicago-ice-trump-bovino-marimar-martinez-crime-border-patrol-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >ICE protesters keep beating Trump in Chicago court, but the battles take a toll — ‘It’s about intimidation’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" >Cook County’s top prosecutor outlines plan to charge ICE agents with crimes</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/12/chicago-area-resident-lawsuit-facebook-ice-tracking-app" target="_blank" >Chicago-area resident sues Trump officials over Facebook shutting down popular ICE sighting page</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Labeled a gang member and deported, longtime Chicagoan tries to restart in his Mexican hometown
summary: <p>Francisco Gonzalez-Jasso, a longtime Little Village resident, didn't know exactly how to make his way back to his childhood home in Torreón, a city in Mexico's northern state of Cahuila. He hadn’t been there in 33 years.</p><p>“I kept asking people on the bus, 'Is Torreón next?' ” Gonzalez-Jasso, 55, says in his native Spanish.</p><p>In Torreón, he took a cab to his old block. But the years had erased his memory of the house. He paced the street, checking the addresses on every door. When he found the right one, he says, the house looked different. It was really small.</p><p>“I started yelling out my brother’s name: Cesar, Cesar,” Gonzalez-Jasso says. “Once I saw his face, I told the taxi driver to leave. Then, I embraced my brother.</p><p>“I was broken.".</p><p>The last time they were together, Cesar, now 50, was 17.</p><p>Gonzalez-Jasso is trying to rebuild his life in Mexico after he was arrested by Border Patrol agents last October in Little Village in front of friends and neighbors. He was deported a few days later. WBEZ has been keeping up with Gonzalez-Jasso after visiting him in Mexico in December, not long after he arrived there.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" He has a large extended family in his hometown but the adjustment back home has been a struggle.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Duilio Rodríguez/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The tall man with a sturdy build was a well-known presence in his Chicago neighborhood for more than three decades. Still, despite not having a criminal record, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security branded him a member of the Latin Kings gang — a tag that has followed him to Mexico.</p><p>Gonzalez-Jasso is among hundreds of people swept up during Operation Midway Blitz, the aggressive Trump administration deportation campaign aimed at clearing “violent criminals” off Chicago-area streets. He also is among immigrants who say they were wrongly accused of being a criminal or having ties to gangs.</p><p>“It’s humiliating for me,” Gonzalez-Jasso says. “I’m not a criminal. I never harmed anyone.”</p><h3>‘This was his home’ </h3><p>Gonzalez-Jasso was known on 26th Street in Little Village as Panchito. His arrest and deportation last fall were a gut punch to neighbors who remember him as a friendly face always ready to lend a hand.</p><p>“I cried, honestly, I cried when I learned that Panchito was arrested,” Carlos Macías, the owner of Carniceria y Taqueria Aguas Calientes on 26th street, said in Spanish. The two have been friends for more than 20 years.</p><p>Also speaking Spanish, Ana Guerrero, a waitress at the <i>taqueria</i> who often served Gonzalez-Jasso, said: “He was like your daily coffee, always here in the mornings before heading to work. He was always very respectful. This was his home.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-960000" name="image-960000"></a> He stepped out to buy a pack of cigarettes. That's when Border Patrol agents arrested him.</p><p>“The saddest thing, and it hurts, is that they grabbed me, they forced me down, pointed a gun at me, in front of people, children.” Gonzalez-Jasso says. “Your world collapses. Your life is over. Tied up, handcuffed, in pain, disappointed. What did I do?”</p><p>He says Border Patrol agents punched him several times as they dragged him to a van. The agents didn’t know his name, didn’t show him a warrant and had no reason to stop him, he says. He hadn’t slept, showered or changed clothes in days. He was in pain from the punches during his arrest, he says.</p><p>He spent two days in bed. It took him several weeks to feel like himself again, he says.</p><p>“I kept thinking, ‘What am I going to do,’” he says. “I was deported like the worst criminal. My reputation is gone.”</p><p>And the home where he was now living wasn’t what he remembered. Over the years, he had lost both his parents and two brothers. The faded curtains and worn furniture were a constant reminder that three decades had passed, that his parents were no longer there to hold things together.</p><p>Gonzalez-Jasso says he felt like an intruder there despite his brother's efforts to make him feel welcome. Cesar was living there with his wife and three children.</p><p>His brother and other relatives had seen the videos of his arrest even before he arrived — making his integration that much harder. deportation, Gonzalez-Jasso is living on a modest pension from his construction work. He shipped his clothes from Chicago and gave away the furniture he left behind. He is trying to get someone to haul his two cars.</p><p>He’s keeping busy remodeling his parents’ home, doing a complete overhaul of the kitchen and the bedrooms.</p><p>But he worries about the violence in Mexico. One of his brothers disappeared years ago and was never found.</p><p>Once in a while, he replays the video of his arrest. It’s painful to hear the sounds — the whistles, a woman yelling <i>“la migra”</i> — and to see himself surrounded by Border Patrol agents.</p><p>Gonzalez-Jasso wants to clear his name so everyone knows he’s not a gang member. But he doesn’t know where to start.</p><p>And he misses his Little Village friends and neighbors. Some of them recently traveled to Mexico to see him for a few days. They aren't his blood relatives. But they were his family.</p><p>In Chicago, he says, his voice cracking, “There are many people who love me. And I miss them.”</p>

title: Judge orders 32 detainees released over ICE consent decree violations, but some have already been deported
summary: <p>A federal judge ordered the release Friday of 32 people arrested during Operation Midway Blitz because of violations of a long-standing consent decree, including two people caught up in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/01/massive-immigration-raid-on-chicago-apartment-building-leaves-residents-reeling-i-feel-defeated" target="_blank" >military-style raid</a> on a South Shore apartment complex<b> </b>last fall.</p><p>Many of the 32 people have already been released or deported, though. Regardless, U.S. District Judge Jeffrey<b> </b>Cummings<b> </b>said he wants the federal government to release those remaining in its custody by noon<b> </b>Thursday. He offered to let the feds argue for a “reasonable”<b> </b>extension of time,<b> </b>if necessary.</p><p>He also told them,<b> </b>“there’s no need to hold them until March 5 if they can be released more quickly.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/04/chicago-trump-immigration-deportation-ice-raid-south-shore-midway-blitz" >Building owner OK’d Trump administration’s raid of Chicago apartment complex, court records show</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The judge said he’s still considering how to rule in the cases of five additional people, meaning his final written order could apply to as many as 37 individuals. He ruled from the bench Friday during a hearing at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse.</p><p>Cummings said the individuals should be released “on their own recognizance, without conditions and without bond.” He considered the circumstances of roughly 50 people, following recent guidance and restrictions handed down by a federal appeals court.</p><p>The judge found that many of the people now set for release were arrested without a warrant, and that agents lacked probable cause to believe they would escape.</p><p>The ruling revolves around the so-called Castanon Nava settlement agreement. It restricts the ability of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, and anyone working with them, to make warrantless arrests in Illinois and nearby states.</p><p>Mark Fleming, the associate director of federal litigation for the National Immigrant Justice Center who represents plaintiffs in the case, said “our singular goal right now is to get as many people out, where there were violations, as possible.”</p><p>“We sense an urgency because people have been stuck, unlawfully, in detention for months now,” Fleming told reporters after court.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/01/massive-immigration-raid-on-chicago-apartment-building-leaves-residents-reeling-i-feel-defeated" >Massive immigration raid on Chicago apartment building leaves residents reeling: ‘I feel defeated’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Twenty-one of the 32 have already either been released or deported, Fleming later told the Chicago Sun-Times. That leaves 11 who will now released, while 10 more could also have restrictions on their freedom lifted.</p><p>The judge's order applies to Jose Miguel<b> </b>Jimenez<b> </b>and Jeickson Delgado<b> </b>Avila.<b> </b>They were among 37 detained during the Sept. 30 raid of the apartment complex at 7500 S. South Shore Drive.</p><p>The raid became an early flashpoint during Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign.</p><p>Federal agents descended on the 130-unit complex from helicopters and used flashbang grenades to burst through doors. Residents reported seeing men, women and children pulled from apartments and zip-tied, some of them naked.</p><p>Records have shown the building’s owner, Trinity Flood, and property manager, Corey Oliver, gave <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/04/chicago-trump-immigration-deportation-ice-raid-south-shore-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >“verbal and written consent”</a> to search the building. Agents only checked units “not legally rented or leased at the time,” documents show.</p><p>Federal officials have said the surrounding South Shore neighborhood was<b> </b>“a location known to be frequented” by the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua. However, crime in the three blocks surrounding the South Shore complex has fallen in recent years.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/11/federal-appeals-court-blocks-release-hundreds-but-trump-still-loses-mixed-immigration-ruling" >Federal appeals court blocks release of hundreds, but Trump still loses in mixed immigration ruling</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Cummings in November also entered an order that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/12/federal-judge-orders-release-hundreds-feds-deportation-midway-blitz-warrantless-arrests" target="_blank" >aimed to release</a> as many as 615 people who were held by immigration authorities and did not pose a high safety risk.</p><p>The 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/11/federal-appeals-court-blocks-release-hundreds-but-trump-still-loses-mixed-immigration-ruling" target="_blank" >blocked that order</a> in December but said many people could still be released if a judge made<b> </b>individual determinations about whether their arrests violated the settlement agreement.</p><p>That’s how Cummings spent the bulk of Friday’s hearing, which lasted roughly three hours.</p><p><i>Contributing: Sophie Sherry</i></p>
author: Jon Seidel
